title: World welcomes 2026 with fireworks after year of Trump and turmoil
description: While a fragile truce took hold in devastated Gaza, violence in Sudan continued unabated.
article_text: Revellers around the world toasted the start of 2026, bidding farewell on Wednesday to a volatile year when temperatures soared, US President Donald Trump upended global trade, and the brutal conflict in Ukraine raged on. While a fragile truce took hold in devastated Gaza, violence in Sudan continued unabated. A new American pope was installed at the Vatican, the world lost pioneering zoologist Jane Goodall, and Labubu dolls sparked a worldwide frenzy. In Sydney, partygoers paused for a minute of silence to remember the victims of the mass shooting on Bondi Beach before fireworks lit up the skies at the stroke of midnight. Heavily armed police patrolled the shoreline, packed with hundreds of thousands of people, barely two weeks after 15 people were gunned down at a Jewish festival in Australia's deadliest mass shooting for almost 30 years. The famed Sydney Harbour Bridge was bathed in white light to symbolise peace. Pacific nations including Kiribati and New Zealand were the first to see in 2026, with Seoul and Tokyo following Sydney in celebrations that make their way around the globe with each passing hour. In Hong Kong, a major New Year fireworks display was cancelled in homage to 161 people killed in a fire in November that engulfed several apartment blocks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country was "10 percent" away from a deal to end the fighting, soon to reach the four-year mark. Russia's Vladimir Putin meanwhile used his traditional New Year address to urge his compatriots to believe that Moscow would deliver a victory in Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. In the Ukrainian city of Vyshgorod, beauty salon manager Daria Lushchyk said the war had made her work "hell" but that her clients were still showing up. "Nothing can stop our Ukrainian girls from coming in and getting themselves glam," Lushchyk said. - Tariffs and fragile truce - This year has brought a mix of stress and excitement for many, war for others still -- and a daring jewel heist at the Louvre. Pop megastar Taylor Swift got engaged to her American football player boyfriend Travis Kelce, and K-pop heartthrobs BTS made their long-awaited return. Trump returned as US president in January, launching a tariff blitz that sent global trade and world stock markets into meltdown. As he prepared to host a New Year's party at his lavish Florida home, the Republican president launched a broadside at Oscar-winning actor George Clooney. After two years of war that left much of the Gaza Strip in ruins, pressure from Trump helped land a fragile ceasefire between Israel and Hamas in October -- though both sides have accused each other of flagrant violations. "We bid farewell to 2025 with deep sorrow and grief," said Gaza City resident Shireen Al-Kayali. "We lost a lot of people and our possessions. We lived a difficult and harsh life, displaced from one city to another, under bombardment and in terror." In contrast, there was optimism despite abiding internal challenges in Syria, where residents of the capital Damascus celebrated a full year since the fall of Bashar al-Assad. "There is no fear, the people are happy, all of Syria is one and united, and God willing…it will be a good year for the people and the wise leadership," marketing manager Sahar al-Said, 33, told AFP as bells rang in Damascus. In Dubai, thousands of revellers queued for up to nine hours for a spectacular fireworks and laser display at the Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building. Revellers popped champagne near the Eiffel Tower in Paris, Bulgaria adopted the euro, and huge crowds danced at Edinburgh's Hogmanay street party. More than two million people are expected to pack Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana Beach for what authorities have called the world's biggest New Year's Eve party. In the US capital, the Washington Monument will be lit up to kick off America's 250th birthday celebration year. And in New York, thousands gathered in freezing temperatures amid tight security for the traditional ball drop in Times Square. The coming 12 months promise to be full of sports, space and questions over artificial intelligence. Athletes will gather in Italy in February for the Winter Olympics. And for a few weeks in June and July, 48 nations will compete in the biggest football World Cup in history in the United States, Mexico and Canada. NASA is planning a crewed mission to circle the moon during a 10-day flight, more than 50 years since the last Apollo lunar mission. And after years of unbridled enthusiasm, AI is facing scrutiny, and nervous investors are questioning whether the boom might now resemble a market bubble.

title: What 2026 holds for music: New albums, tours and resistance to AI
description: As 2025 draws to a close and year-end round-ups give way to anticipation, attention is turning to what 2026 may hold for the music world—from album releases and festival line-ups to questions about live returns and the growing role of artificial intelligence.
article_text: As 2025 draws to a close and year-end round-ups give way to anticipation, attention is turning to what 2026 may hold for the music world—from album releases and festival line-ups to questions about live returns and the growing role of artificial intelligence. The past year felt transitional in many respects. With relatively few major A-list releases and a conspicuous lull during the summer, the mainstream charts remained unusually static. Just three songs dominated the number one position for much of the year: Taylor Swift's "Fate of Ophelia", Huntr/x's "Golden" and Alex Warren's "Ordinary". Beyond algorithm-driven playlists, however, audiences showed growing interest in music that pushed boundaries. Geese earned critical praise for "Getting Killed", while Spanish pop star Rosalía released "Lux", an ambitious album blending flamenco, opera, hip-hop and experimental rhythms. Former Little Mix member Jade Thirlwall explored pop stardom with "That's Showbiz, Baby!", and Lily Allen reasserted her lyrical sharpness with "West End Girl". Looking ahead, 2026 will see Glastonbury Festival take a fallow year, but the festival circuit remains packed. Reading and Leeds Festival has announced headliners including Fontaines D C, Florence + The Machine, Dave, Charli XCX, Raye and Chase & Status. Elsewhere, Mighty Hoopla will feature Lily Allen and Scissor Sisters, while Latitude Festival has booked Lewis Capaldi and David Byrne. End of the Road Festival, meanwhile, will host Pulp and CMAT. One of the summer's biggest bookings is set for London's BST Festival, where Pitbull will headline on July 10, joined by special guest Kesha. Speculation also continues around Oasis. After concluding a high-profile comeback tour in Mexico, frontman Liam Gallagher hinted at a possible return. Rumours persist of a Knebworth House show—site of the band's iconic 1996 concerts—though there is also talk of a pause, particularly as guitarist Bonehead undergoes treatment for prostate cancer. In a statement closing their 2025 tour, the band described an upcoming "period of reflection". Alongside touring and releases, the music industry continues to grapple with artificial intelligence. AI tools are now routinely used in studios for tasks such as isolating vocals or restoring recordings. Controversy flared late in 2025 following allegations that British dance act Haven used AI to replicate Jorja Smith's voice. Streaming platform Deezer has estimated that a third of the music uploaded to its service is now AI-generated. A backlash is also taking shape. Producer Jack Antonoff has spoken about recording with live, imperfect instruments as a response to overly polished pop. Recent releases by Miley Cyrus, Olivia Dean and Skye Newman similarly lean toward organic sounds reminiscent of 1970s pop and soul. Surveys suggest listeners increasingly want transparency around AI use in music. As debates continue, some have even proposed labels identifying recordings made entirely by human musicians—an inversion of the familiar parental advisory sticker. Whether such measures gain traction may become one of the defining questions of music in 2026.

title: Mamdani takes over as New York mayor
description: He is New York's first Muslim mayor.
article_text: Zohran Mamdani, the young upstart of the US left, was sworn in Thursday to take over as New York mayor for a term sure to see him cross swords with President Donald Trump. After the clocks struck midnight, bringing in 2026, Mamdani took his oath of office at an abandoned subway stop to begin managing the United States' largest city. He is New York's first Muslim mayor. His office said the understated venue beneath City Hall reflected his commitment to working people, after the 34-year-old Democrat campaigned on promises to address the soaring cost of living. "This is truly the honor and the privilege of a lifetime," Mamdani told reporters after taking his oath. But it remains to be seen if Mamdani -- virtually unknown a year ago -- can deliver on his ambitious agenda, which envisions rent freezes, universal childcare and free public buses. Once an election is over, "symbolism only goes so far with voters. Results begin to matter a whole lot more," New York University lecturer John Kane said. How Trump behaves could be a decisive factor. The Republican, himself a New Yorker, has repeatedly criticized Mamdani, but the pair held surprisingly cordial talks at the White House in November. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, said the meeting "couldn't have gone better from Mamdani's perspective." But he warned their relationship could quickly sour. One flashpoint might be immigration raids as Trump wages an expanding crackdown on migrants across the United States. Mamdani has vowed to protect immigrant communities. Before the November vote, the president also threatened to slash federal funding for New York if it picked Mamdani, whom he called a "communist lunatic." The mayor-elect has said he believes Trump is a fascist. Mamdani's private swearing-in to start his four-year term was performed by New York Attorney General Letitia James, who successfully prosecuted Trump for fraud. A larger, ceremonial inauguration is scheduled later Thursday with speeches from left-wing allies Senator Bernie Sanders and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Around 4,000 ticketed guests are expected to attend the event outside City Hall. Mamdani's team has also organized a block party that it says will enable tens of thousands of people to watch the ceremony at streetside viewing areas along Broadway. In a first for the city, Mamdani is using several Korans to be sworn in as mayor -- two from his family and one that belonged to Puerto Rico-born Black writer Arturo Schomburg, The New York Times reported. The new job comes with a change of address as he swaps his rent-controlled apartment in the borough of Queens for the luxurious mayor's residence in Manhattan. Some had wondered if he would move to the official mansion given his campaigning on affordability issues. Mamdani said he is doing so mainly for security reasons. Born in Uganda to a family of Indian origin, Mamdani moved to New York at age seven and enjoyed an elite upbringing with only a relatively brief stint in politics, becoming a member of the New York State Assembly before being elected mayor. Compensating for his inexperience, he is surrounding himself with seasoned aides recruited from past mayoral administrations and former US president Joe Biden's government. Mamdani has also opened dialogue with business leaders, some of whom predicted a massive exodus of wealthy New Yorkers if he won. Real estate leaders have debunked those claims. As a defender of Palestinian rights, he will have to reassure the Jewish community of his inclusive leadership. Recently, one of his hires resigned after it was revealed she had posted antisemitic tweets years ago.

title: Democracy cannot survive when its defenders are set on fire
description: "I can't breathe anymore. There's too much smoke. I'm inside. You are killing me."
article_text: "I can't breathe anymore. There's too much smoke. I'm inside. You are killing me." This was the social media post made by The Daily Star 's Zyma Islam in the early hours of December 19. When I first saw the post, it sent a chill down my spine. I could not believe my eyes. Was this really happening? Two media buildings, located within a few hundred yards of each other, were set ablaze that night. They housed Bangladesh's two most influential daily newspapers: Prothom Alo and The Daily Star . These were not some secretive arson attacks. They happened right in front of thousands, both on the streets and those watching live on social media. The journalist I quoted was trapped inside along with some of her colleagues. Although they were eventually rescued by the firefighters and security forces, the event left a deep scar on the nation's collective psyche. The reason for this lunacy is so absurd, so detached from logic, that no sane observer can plausibly connect cause and consequence. In every measurable sense, these papers' circulation, reach, credibility, and agenda-setting powers are unrivalled pillars of Bangladesh's news industry. For decades, they have shaped public discourse, built narratives around national events, and set the professional standards by which journalism in Bangladesh is judged. Even those who resent their editorial stance routinely rely on their coverage for verification of facts, simply because hardly any comparable alternative exists that combines professionalism, consistency, and institutional memory. That is precisely why they were under attack. Both Prothom Alo and The Daily Star are unapologetically liberal and secular in orientation. From their inception, this has earned them the hostility of ultra-conservative factions that see secularism not as a constitutional principle but as an existential threat. At the same time, it would be disingenuous to pretend that these papers have always practised immaculate impartiality. There were moments where their coverage in certain respects didn't meet the lofty standard set for journalism. Smoke signals about Bangladesh’s future But complete neutrality in journalism is an illusion, not a realistic benchmark. In every society, media institutions reflect values, worldviews, and editorial judgments. The relevant question is not whether absolute impartiality exists, but whether professional standards, fact-checking, source verification, and editorial accountability are upheld. On that score, these two dailies do not merely meet the threshold; they exceed it. That is why they became indispensable institutions rather than partisan actors. Their credibility did not shield them from power. In fact, it made them frequent targets. Every government in Bangladesh has resented these newspapers for one reason or another, but the hostility reached its zenith during Sheikh Hasina's rule (2009–2024). Her regime, marked by systemic corruption, enforced disappearances, extrajudicial killings, and the decimation of democratic institutions, found its most persistent critics in these two outlets. Hasina made her contempt explicit. She publicly stated that she avoided reading Prothom Alo and The Daily Star . Their reporters were routinely barred from attending press briefings. Their editors, Matiur Rahman and Mahfuz Anam, faced lawsuits, intimidation, and financial strangulation. Advertising pressure was applied through state influence over major companies. There were even credible fears that the regime wanted to engineer a hostile takeover of these papers, echoing how India's major business groups aligned with the Modi government absorbed influential media outlets. Their "crime" was simple: they reported corruption and human rights abuses when silence was the safer option. Here lies the central paradox. Sheikh Hasina was arguably New Delhi's most reliable partner in South Asia. Her government systematically addressed India's security and strategic concerns, often at the expense of Bangladesh's own democratic accountability. In return, India provided unwavering diplomatic cover, shielding Hasina's brutal dictatorial regime from international scrutiny, particularly from Western powerful countries. Even after Hasina's fall in August 2024, India continued to provide her material and political support. Hasina fled to India and has since been allowed to issue vitriolic statements against Bangladesh's interim government frequently. Numerous Awami League leaders and former ministers are also reportedly residing in India, often appearing on Indian talk shows and digital platforms to denounce the current political transition. There is also a pervasive though unsubstantiated belief in Bangladesh that India's intelligence agency, RAW, which allegedly penetrated multiple sectors of Bangladesh during Hasina's rule, is now collaborating with fallen Awami League operatives to destabilise the country. Moreover, under the laws of Bangladesh, Sheikh Hasina has been convicted in absentia and is therefore legally liable to face justice in the country. Yet India has shown no indication of cooperating with any extradition process or facilitating her return. These dynamics have also emboldened local radical actors. Younger political figures, student wings such as Bangladesh Islami Chhatrashibir, and even emerging groups like the National Citizen Party (NCP) have adopted openly confrontational rhetoric towards India. But getting back to the point, if the two newspapers were Hasina's most consistent critics, and she sought to hurt or attack them repeatedly, how could they also be "pro-fascist" or "pro-India"? This claim collapses under basic scrutiny. Yes, there were moments when these papers softened their criticism of Hasina, but those were dictated by a survival instinct, not any ideological alignment.A regime that weaponised laws, courts, regulators, advertisers, and police left little room for open defiance. Even then, these newspapers continued to expose major corruption scandals and rights violations, often at great institutional risk. How 2025 thinned our cultural space So, what their current branding as "acolytes" of Hasina or India actually reflects is something more dangerous: manufactured hatred. Following Hasina's fall, some Islamist parties, long suppressed under the guise of a "war on terror," re-entered public life with renewed confidence. Social media influencers sympathetic to extremist views pushed a toxic narrative: that Prothom Alo and The Daily Star were ideological extensions of Indian hegemony, allegedly poisoning Muslim minds through secular liberalism. These narratives blended fragments of truth with deliberate falsehoods. In a society plagued by illiteracy, algorithmic amplification, and rising religious radicalism, such claims spread rapidly. Over time, a segment of the population was led to view these newspapers in adversarial terms, creating an opening that vested interest groups were quick to exploit. The assassination of Sharif Osman Hadi became the spark. Though there is no evidence linking the newspapers to the killing, they became symbolic targets. Burning down major narrative-building institutions accomplishes multiple goals, including weakening ideological enemies, undermining the democratic process, and creating fear and chaos in the country. Perhaps most disturbing was the role or absence of the state. Security forces were deployed late, despite prior intelligence indicating imminent violence after Hadi's assassination. The inaction suggested either gross incompetence or tacit consent. Some observers are quite confident that certain elements within the interim government were themselves involved in this planned inaction. The major reason, one may imagine, is their alleged alignment with political actors who stand to lose ground or power in a proper democratic transition. Meanwhile, threats and mob violence continue. These are not isolated events. They are symptoms of a state losing its monopoly over violence while the country is being destabilised in the process. In this struggle for power, ideology, and control, there is only one consistent loser: Bangladesh. Businesses stall. Investment retreats. Social trust erodes. Institutions crumble. Right now, what we need is not more manufactured enemies, but a free, fair, and timely election leading to the return of democratic governance rooted in accountability and pluralism. Silencing narratives will not save Bangladesh or restore faith. Only democracy and the rule of law can. And democracy cannot survive when its most ardent defenders—newspapers like The Daily Star and Prothom Alo —are set on fire. title: Crisis-hit Sri Lanka's inflation falls way below target
description: Sri Lanka has been slowly emerging from its worst economic meltdown in 2022
article_text: Sri Lanka's inflation rose 2.1 percent last year, well below its target of five percent, the central bank said Thursday, but projected a "gradual acceleration" in 2026. While low inflation may appear positive for consumers, a rate below the central bank's target signals underlying economic issues including weak consumer demand. Sri Lanka has been slowly emerging from its worst economic meltdown in 2022, when it ran out of foreign exchange reserves to pay for essential imports such as food, fuel and medicines. But it was hit hard in November by a cyclone that killed at least 643 people -- with another 183 listed as missing -- and affected more than 10 percent of the island's population. The storm caused an estimated $4.1 billion in direct physical damage to buildings and agriculture, according to the World Bank. The Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI), the official measure of inflation, rose to 195.8 in December from 191.7 a year earlier, marking a 2.1 percent increase. "Inflation projections... (since) November 2025 indicate a gradual acceleration of inflation towards the target of five percent in the period ahead," the central bank said. Sri Lanka has secured a $206 million emergency loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to meet part of the relief costs. The country has been stabilising its fragile economy with the help of a $2.9 billion IMF bailout agreed in early 2023.

title: Drugmakers raise US prices on 350 medicines despite pressure from Trump
description: The number of price increases for 2026 is up from the same point last year
article_text: Drugmakers plan to raise US prices on at least 350 branded medications including vaccines against COVID, RSV and shingles and blockbuster cancer treatment Ibrance, even as the Trump administration pressures them for cuts, according to data provided exclusively by healthcare research firm 3 Axis Advisors. The number of price increases for 2026 is up from the same point last year, when drugmakers unveiled plans for raises on more than 250 drugs. The median of this year's price hikes is around 4 percent - in line with 2025. The increases do not reflect any rebates to pharmacy benefit managers and other discounts. DRUGMAKERS ALSO CUT SOME PRICES Drugmakers also plan to cut the list prices on around nine drugs. That includes a more than 40 percent cut for Boehringer Ingelheim's diabetes drug Jardiance and three related treatments. Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly, which sell Jardiance together, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the reason for the price cuts. Jardiance is among the 10 drugs for which the US government negotiated a lower price for the Medicare program for people aged 65 and older in 2026. Under those negotiations, Boehringer and Lilly slashed the Jardiance price by two-thirds. US patients currently pay by far the most for prescription medicines, often nearly three times more than in other developed nations, and Trump has been pressuring drugmakers to lower their prices to what patients pay in similarly wealthy nations. The increases on 350 medicines come even as Trump has struck deals with 14 drugmakers on prices of some of their medicines for the government's Medicaid program for low-income Americans and for cash payers. Pfizer, Sanofi, Boehringer Ingelheim, Novartis and GSK are among those companies and also plan to raise prices on some drugs on January 1. "These deals are being announced as transformative when, in fact, they really just nibble around the margins in terms of what is really driving high prices for prescription drugs in the US," said Dr. Benjamin Rome, a health policy researcher at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston. Rome said the companies seem to be maximizing prices while negotiating discounts behind the scenes with health and drug insurers and then setting yet another price for direct-to-consumer cash-pay sales. Pfizer announced the most list price hikes, on around 80 different drugs including cancer drug Ibrance, migraine pill Nurtec, and COVID treatment Paxlovid, as well as some administered in hospitals such as morphine and hydromorphone. Most of Pfizer's increases are below 10 percent, except for a 15 percent hike of COVID vaccine Comirnaty, while some of its relatively inexpensive hospital drugs saw more than four-fold increases. Pfizer said in a statement it had adjusted the average list price of its innovative medicines and vaccines for 2026 below the overall rate of inflation. "The modest increase is necessary to support investments that allow us to continue to discover and deliver new medicines as well as address increased costs throughout our business," the company said. Larger US drug price increases were once far more common. Drugmakers have scaled them back due to criticism from lawmakers and new government policies, such as penalizing companies that charge Medicare program prices that rise faster than inflation. European drugmaker GSK plans to increase prices on around 20 drugs and vaccines from 2 percent to 8.9 percent. The drugmaker said it is committed to reasonable prices and the hikes are needed to support scientific innovation. Sanofi and Novartis did not respond to requests for comment. More price hikes and cuts can be expected in early January, which is historically the biggest month for drugmakers to raise prices. 3 Axis is a consulting firm that works with pharmacist groups, health plans and some pharmaceutical industry-related groups on drug pricing and supply chain issues. It is a related entity to, and shares staff with, drug pricing non-profit 46brooklyn.

title: Sabalenka wants 'Battle of the Sexes' rematch and revenge
description: World number one Aryna Sabalenka Thursday said she wants a rematch of her "Battle of the Sexes" showdown with Nick Kyrgios so she can get revenge.
article_text: World number one Aryna Sabalenka Thursday said she wants a rematch of her "Battle of the Sexes" showdown with Nick Kyrgios so she can get revenge. Australia's Kyrgios beat the Belarusian 6-3, 6-3 in a highly-publicised showdown in Dubai last Sunday, with modified rules that divided fans. Sabalenka's side of the court was reduced in size by nine percent in an attempt to restrict Kyrgios' power and speed advantage, while each player only received one serve. "I think I would definitely do it again," she said ahead of the Brisbane International, her season-opening tournament as she prepares for the Australian Open on January 18. "I love revenge and I don't like to leave it the way it is." While keen to face-off with Kyrgios again, Sabalenka said she would want a full court and two serves. "I think for the next match we will come up with a different format," she said. "Before the match I didn't realise I would have to adjust and it was a bit tricky for me. I think I would keep the full court but I would take two serves. That would even our level a lot more. "I always say that when you are losing, you are learning and I learned a lot about his game," she added. "I would do it again. I need revenge." The contest bore little resemblance to the era-defining 1973 "Battle of the Sexes" encounter between Billie Jean King and Bobby Riggs. Back then, there was more at stake with the nascent women's professional tour, set up by King, fighting for legitimacy and prize money for female players far lower than for the men. King, one of the all-time greats of the women's game who was at the peak of her powers, saw off the 55-year-old Riggs, a top player in his day, 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 in Houston. The Sabalenka-Kyrgios showdown faced backlash, with some calling it a "money grab" while others said it did little to advance the women's game. But Sabalenka said she felt exhibition tennis, like the Kyrgios contest, was important. "I think it's really important for tennis to keep it interesting, keep it fresh, keep it new, keep it fun," she said. She added that she was proud of her part in the "Battle of the Sexes", despite Kyrgios barely playing in recent years and ranked a lowly 671. "I am happy that I was able to challenge him, make him work and make him physically get tired and mentally get tired," she said. "I felt really excited to see a man getting tired and going for his full game. It was a really cool experience." The Brisbane International starts on Sunday with Sabalenka's sights set on a third Australian Open title after winning in 2023 and 2024. She was beaten in the Melbourne Park final last year by Madison Keys.

title: Israel says it 'will enforce' ban on 37 NGOs in Gaza
description: The groups will now be required to cease their operations by March 1
article_text: Israel said on Thursday that 37 international NGOs operating in Gaza had not complied with a deadline to meet "security and transparency standards," in particular disclosing information on their Palestinian staff, and that it "will enforce" a ban on their activities. The groups will now be required to cease their operations by March 1, which the United Nations has warned will exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in the war-ravaged Palestinian territory. "Organisations that have failed to meet required security and transparency standards will have their licenses suspended," the Ministry of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism said in a statement on Thursday. Several NGOS have said the requirements contravene international humanitarian law or endanger their independence, while Israel has faced international criticism in the run-up to the deadline. Israel says the new regulation aims to prevent bodies it accuses of supporting terrorism from operating in the Palestinian territories. "The primary failure identified was the refusal to provide complete and verifiable information regarding their employees, a critical requirement designed to prevent the infiltration of terrorist operatives into humanitarian structures," the ministry said. In March, Israel gave a ten-month deadline to NGOs to comply with the new rules, which demand the "full disclosure of personnel, funding sources, and operational structures." The deadline expired on Wednesday. The 37 NGOs "were formally notified that their licenses would be revoked as of January 1, 2026, and that they must complete the cessation of their activities by March 1, 2026," the ministry said Thursday. - 'Weaponisation of bureaucracy' - Minister of Diaspora Affairs and Combating Antisemitism Amichai Chikli said "the message is clear: humanitarian assistance is welcome — the exploitation of humanitarian frameworks for terrorism is not". Numerous prominent humanitarian organisations have been hit by the ban, including Doctors Without Borders (MSF), World Vision International and Oxfam, according to the list provided by the ministry. In the case of MSF, Israel accused it of having two employees who were members of Palestinian militant groups Islamic Jihad and Hamas. MSF said earlier this week that the request to share a list of its staff "may be in violation of Israel's obligations under international humanitarian law" and said it "would never knowingly employ people engaging in military activity". On Thursday, 18 Israel-based left-wing NGOs denounced the decision to ban their international peers, saying "the new registration framework violates core humanitarian principles of independence and neutrality." "This weaponisation of bureaucracy institutionalises barriers to aid and forces vital organisations to suspend operations," they said. On Wednesday, United Nations rights chief Volker Turk described Israel's decision as "outrageous", calling on states to urgently insist Israel shift course. "Such arbitrary suspensions make an already intolerable situation even worse for the people of Gaza," he said. UN Palestinian refugee agency chief Philippe Lazzarini said the move sets a "dangerous precedent". "Failing to push back against attempts to control the work of aid organisations will further undermine the basic humanitarian principles of neutrality, independence, impartiality and humanity underpinning aid work across the world," he said on X. On Tuesday, the foreign ministers of 10 countries, including France and the United Kingdom, urged Israel to "guarantee access" to aid in the Gaza Strip, where they said the humanitarian situation remains "catastrophic". A fragile ceasefire has been in place in Gaza since October, following a deadly war waged by Israel in response to Hamas's unprecedented attack on Israeli territory on October 7, 2023. Conditions for the civilian population in the Gaza Strip remain dire, with nearly 80 percent of buildings destroyed or damaged by the war, according to UN data. About 1.5 million of Gaza's more than two million residents have lost their homes, said Amjad Al-Shawa, director of the Palestinian NGO Network in Gaza.

title: Dozens killed, 100 injured in fire at Swiss ski resort bar, police say
description: Witnesses say ceiling caught fire
article_text: Dozens of people were killed and around 100 injured, most of them seriously, in a fire during a New Year's Eve party in the resort town of Crans-Montana , officials said on Thursday. Fire broke out at 1.30am (0030 GMT) in a bar called "Le Constellation" in the resort in south-western Switzerland, which locals said was popular with teenagers. The cause of the blaze, which was initially reported as an explosion, remains unclear but authorities said it appeared to be an accident rather than an attack. Swiss police said "tens" of people were presumed dead with around 100 injured, and the Italian foreign ministry said information from Swiss police indicated about 40 deaths. Swiss officials declined to give a specific figure. "There were people screaming, and then people lying on the ground, probably dead," said 21-year-old local Samuel Rapp, who saw the aftermath of the fire. "They had jackets over their faces—well, that's what I saw, nothing more." Video footage showed lines of ambulances queuing and helicopters landing to take victims to nearby hospitals and specialist burns units in other Swiss cities. Two young French women who said they were in the bar told France's BFM TV that they saw the fire start in the basement section of the club after a bottle containing "birthday candles" was held up too close to the wooden ceiling. "The fire spread across the ceiling super quickly," one of the two women, who identified themselves as Emma and Albane, told BFM TV. The pair said they were able to climb a narrow staircase to the ground floor and escape the building. Minutes later, the fire had reached the ground floor too, they said. BFM showed video of a waitress carrying a champagne bottle with a lit 'fountain candle' through the bar, in line with the account, but the video did not show the fire taking hold. Video footage verified by Reuters showed fire spreading from the building, with people outside the club, some of them running and screaming. VICTIMS COME FROM SEVERAL COUNTRIES Italy's ambassador to Switzerland, Gian Lorenzo Cornado, told Sky TG24 local authorities had told him the blaze was started by someone letting off a firework inside the bar which set fire to the ceiling. He was in Crans-Montana, where he said a number of Italians had gathered seeking information about missing relatives or friends. He declined to say if there were any Italian victims but witnesses said many of those in the bar appeared to be from other countries. Witnesses described injured being treated in improvised triage centres set up in a nearby bar and in a branch of UBS bank and said many suffered after coming out of the heat of the bar into the freezing night air. "And then it was just ambulances coming back and forth as much as possible," said Dominic Dubois, who witnessed the frantic scenes as the bodies were brought out. A waiter in a restaurant near to the bar who declined to be named said that first responders approached staff overnight asking for tablecloths to cover the bodies to conceal them from onlookers. On Thursday morning, hours after the explosion, footage from the street outside showed the area cordoned off, with forensic tents behind white screens set up in front of the bar, one of many in Crans-Montana, a fashionable ski centre with an array of boutiques, luxury hotels and restaurants. "I know someone who might have been among the victims and I can't reach her. I'm very worried," said local resident Karine Spreng. "I'm going to try to contact other people who know this woman to see if she is still alive." The daytime scene, with small groups of people, some in tears or carrying flowers, was a stark contrast to the panic and confusion that officials said faced first responders who arrived when the alarm was raised. "The first responders – the firefighters and police officers – arrived at a scene of chaos, at a dramatic scene," Stephane Ganzer, head of security for Valais canton, told reporters. He said some of the victims were from other countries, hundreds of personnel were working on the case and a helpline had been opened for relatives. Officials said the grim task of identifying badly burned bodies would take a considerable time. "I can't hide from you that we are all shaken by what happened overnight in Crans," the canton's head of police, Frederic Gisler, told the press conference. "Our count is about 100 injured, most seriously, and unfortunately tens of people are presumed dead," he said, adding that patients had been dispatched to hospitals in Sion, Lausanne, Geneva and Zurich. Local prosecutor Beatrice Pilloud said a full investigation had been opened into the incident at the bar, which Swiss company records indicated was owned by a French couple. "At the moment we are considering this a fire and we are not considering the possibility of an attack," she told a press conference. Swiss Federal President Guy Parmelin expressed shock at the scale of the disaster, which came less than a year after a fire in a club in North Macedonia killed 59 people. "What was meant to be a moment of joy turned, on the first day of the year in Crans-Montana, into mourning that touches the entire country and far beyond," he said on the social media platform X, expressing condolences. The foreign ministers of neighbouring Italy and Germany and other countries including the United States expressed condolences but there was no immediate confirmation of the nationality of any of the victims. Prosecutor Pilloud said authorities were trying to get the bodies of the victims to their families. "A lot of resources have been put into forensics to identify the victims. These resources are intended to allow us to get the bodies to the families as soon as possible," she said. Earlier, police said many people were being treated for burns and that the area had been completely closed off, with a no-fly zone imposed over Crans-Montana, which is due to host next year's Alpine World Ski Championships. Authorities said 10 helicopters and 40 ambulances had been deployed.

title: Fire ravages Amsterdam church on 'unsettled' Dutch New Year
description: The cause of the blaze was not immediately clear
article_text: A huge inferno gutted a 19th century Amsterdam church Thursday, as the Netherlands endured an unsettled New Year's Eve with two dead from fireworks and "unprecedented" violence against police. The blaze broke out in the early hours at the Vondelkerk, a tourist attraction that has overlooked one of the city's top parks since 1872. The 50-metre-high (164-foot) tower collapsed and the roof was badly damaged but the structure was expected to remain intact, Amsterdam authorities said. The cause of the blaze was not immediately clear. The head of the Dutch Police Union, Nine Kooiman, reported an "unprecedented amount of violence against police and emergency services" over New Year's Eve. She said she herself had been pelted three times by fireworks and other explosives as she worked a shift in Amsterdam. Shortly after midnight, authorities released a rare country-wide alert on mobile phones warning people not to call overwhelmed emergency services unless lives were at risk. Reports of attacks against police and firefighters were widespread across the country. In the southern city of Breda, people threw petrol bombs at police. Two people, a 17-year-old boy and a 38-year-old man, were killed in fireworks accidents. Three others were seriously injured. The eye hospital in Rotterdam said it had treated 14 patients, including 10 minors, for eye injuries. Two received surgery. It was the last year before an expected ban on unofficial fireworks, so the Dutch bought them in massive quantities. According to the Dutch Pyrotechnics Association, revellers splashed out a record 129 million euros ($151 million) on fireworks. Some areas had been designated firework-free zones, but this appeared to have little effect. An AFP journalist in such a zone in The Hague reported loud bangs until around 3am. In Germany, two 18-year-olds died in the western city of Bielefeld when they set off home-made fireworks that produced "deadly facial injuries," local police said in a statement.

title: Death penalty in Saudi Arabia: What does the law say, and what happens in court?
description: The number of executions in Saudi Arabia is rising at an alarming rate. Recently, two Bangladeshis were executed. In the first six months of this year, Saudi Arabia executed 59 foreign nationals. Questions have repeatedly been raised about the death penalty for drug-related offences, the impact of capital punishment on foreign nationals, and the transparency of judicial proceedings. Amid concerns over allegations of torture, restrictions on access to lawyers, and defendants’ opportunities to defend themselves, the country’s judicial system and its use of the death penalty have once again come under scrutiny. This is the first instalment of a report examining what the country’s laws say and what happens in its courts.
article_text: Nearly fourfold Increase in a decade A record 356 executions were carried out in Saudi Arabia in 2025. A year earlier, in 2024, the number was 345, then the highest in a decade. In 2018, the year after Mohammed bin Salman became crown prince, 149 people were executed. The 2024 figure was more than double that number. Compared with the 90 executions recorded in 2014, the figure had risen nearly fourfold. In the first six months of 2025 alone, 180 people were executed in Saudi Arabia. Amnesty International warned at the time that, if the trend continued, the annual total could approach the record set in 2024. By the end of the year, however, the figure of 356 had surpassed even that record. From January 2014 to June 2025, a total of 1,816 people were executed in Saudi Arabia. Nearly one in every three was sentenced to death solely for a drug-related offence. Human rights organisations say the actual number is higher. In the first six months of the current year, 2026, ESOHR recorded at least 108 executions. According to the organisation, the total number of executions carried out under King Salman bin Abdulaziz and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has reached 2,000. This is a record compared with any previous reign. The final word rests with the judge Saudi Arabia does not have a comprehensive penal code that defines all crimes and their corresponding punishments. Judges have broad discretion to determine what constitutes a crime and what punishment it warrants. They do so based on their own interpretations of Islamic law, or Sharia, and fiqh—the understanding developed by Islamic jurists concerning the interpretation and application of Sharia provisions. Under the country’s system of governance, the Holy Quran and the Sunnah are the ultimate sources of all law. Under Islamic law, crimes are divided into three categories: hudud, qisas and ta’zir. Punishments for the first two categories are prescribed, and they include the death penalty. Hudud refers to prescribed punishments for certain offences, including, in some circumstances, theft, adultery and drinking alcohol. Qisas applies mainly to murder or physical injury and involves retributive punishment. Under specific conditions, victims or the relatives of a deceased victim may grant forgiveness or accept compensation. The third category, ta’zir, covers offences for which punishments are not prescribed under hudud or qisas. It includes acts that undermine public order or the interests of society. In these cases, the judge determines the punishment. Bangladesh asks Saudi Arabia 6 questions over execution of 2 citizens Death sentences in Saudi Arabia reflect a combination of punishments prescribed under Sharia and discretionary decisions under ta’zir. Despite being the harshest and most irreversible form of punishment, the death penalty is left to judicial discretion. Saudi authorities say that capital punishment under ta’zir is “rarely applied”. However, statistics from human rights organisations paint a different picture. Written laws also prescribe the death penalty for certain offences. The principal examples are the 2017 counterterrorism law and the 2005 anti-narcotics law. Under the anti-narcotics law, the death penalty is retained as the primary punishment for several offences. Vague provisions of the counterterrorism law have also been used to sentence people to death on charges such as “endangering national unity”. For offences whose punishments are not specified in any law, judges turn to their interpretations of Sharia. The list of offences punishable by death is also extensive. According to Amnesty International, the death penalty applies not only to murder but also to murder committed in connection with armed robbery, kidnapping or rape. In addition, offences such as treason, rape, kidnapping, witchcraft and sorcery, robbery, torture and attempted murder may carry the death penalty. In drug-related cases, the penalty may apply to trafficking, possession, distribution and even consumption. Under international law, however, the death penalty is permissible only for the “most serious crimes”, such as intentional murder. The Saudi government has told the relevant United Nations body that it imposes the death penalty only for the “most serious crimes”. In February 2021, Saudi authorities announced a draft of a new law titled the Penal Code for Discretionary Sanctions, which was intended to codify ta’zir offences. After analysing a leaked draft, Amnesty International said that, rather than restricting the death penalty, the proposed law would further entrench it. Under the draft, judges would be able to impose death sentences for murder, rape and charges of “blasphemy” and “apostasy”. The draft has not yet been formally passed or brought into force. 2 Bangladeshis executed in Saudi: Parliamentary committee questions consulate’s lapses The country’s highest judicial body is the Supreme Judicial Council. It has 11 members and is headed by the justice minister. The king appoints its members for renewable four-year terms. Under the 2007 Law of the Judiciary, the council oversees the work of courts and judges. The Supreme Court is responsible for reviewing verdicts involving the death penalty, amputation, stoning to death and qisas. The law provides for judicial independence, but according to Amnesty International, judges effectively remain under the control of the executive branch. Judges are appointed by royal decree. Although the law does not explicitly state that judges must be men, all judges in the country are male. Both the Public Prosecution and the state security forces are directly accountable to the king and the crown prince. Saudi researcher Abdullah Alaoudh says the crown prince has turned the judicial system into an instrument of his own control. To this end, he transferred prosecutorial powers—the administrative and legal authority to investigate cases on behalf of the state and bring defendants to trial—from the Interior Ministry to the royal court. He has also removed potential rivals who could exert influence over the judiciary and filled courts with loyalists. According to Amnesty International, the authorities have been able to use the courts to punish critics of the government’s political and economic policies by exploiting judges’ broad discretionary powers and the lack of judicial independence. Execution of 2 Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia: What does the consulate’s letter say? Defendants’ rights do exist on paper. Under the Law of Criminal Procedure, issued by royal decree in November 2013, defendants have the right to legal assistance during both the investigation and trial stages. Torture and other forms of ill-treatment of defendants are prohibited; limits are placed on the duration of pretrial detention; judicial review is mandatory in cases of prolonged detention; and appeals are permitted against all verdicts, including death sentences. In practice, Amnesty International says, safeguards meeting international standards have not been consistently upheld, even in death penalty cases. Cases involving allegations of terrorist activities and political offences are heard by the Specialised Criminal Court. The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has said that this court cannot be considered an independent and impartial tribunal. Promises on paper, a different reality Since 2018, Saudi authorities have repeatedly pledged to reform the use of the death penalty. According to Amnesty International, each time they have either backtracked or failed to implement reforms consistent with international standards. In an interview with The Atlantic on 3 March 2022, the crown prince said that they had abolished everything related to the death penalty except for one category. That category, he said, was set out in the Holy Quran, and there was nothing they could do about it. The crown prince has also repeatedly given public assurances that the death penalty would be retained only for murder and abolished for offences for which Sharia does not mandate capital punishment, such as drug-related crimes. In other words, death sentences would no longer be imposed on the basis of ta’zir. Yet announcements by the Saudi Press Agency itself indicate that executions for ta’zir offences continue. In January 2021, Saudi Arabia’s Human Rights Commission announced on social media that executions for drug-related offences had been suspended. This unofficial moratorium was lifted in 2023, after which executions resumed in cases that had previously been put on hold. Nearly half of all death sentences based on judicial discretion Amnesty International analysed the legal basis for death sentences announced between January 2014 and June 2025. It found that 862 executions, or 47.5 per cent, were based on ta’zir. Of these, 597 (69.3 per cent) were solely for drug-related offences, while 135 (15.7 per cent) were solely for offences related to “terrorism”. The figures over time reveal the following pattern: from 2014 to 2018, roughly half of all death sentences were based on hudud or qisas, with the other half based on ta’zir. In 2019, the share of ta’zir cases jumped to around 71 per cent. That year, the Saudi Press Agency reported 130 executions based on ta’zir, including 84 people executed solely for drug-related offences. The proportion of ta’zir-based executions fell between 2020 and 2023, which Amnesty International believes may partly be attributable to the moratorium on executions for drug-related offences. In 2024, however, 40.9 per cent of executions were again carried out on the basis of ta’zir, while the legal basis for another 11.3 per cent remained unknown. That year, 122 people were executed under ta’zir solely for drug-related offences, nearly twice the figure for 2015. From January to June 2025 alone, the number stood at 118. An expansive definition of ‘terrorism’ and the punishment of dissent Alongside drug-related offences, “terrorism” is the second major category. According to Amnesty International, Saudi Arabia uses extremely vague definitions of “terrorism”, “terrorist offences” and “terrorist organisations” to impose death sentences even in cases that do not involve intentional killing. The aim, the organisation says, is to suppress dissent. Using vague provisions of the 2017 counterterrorism law, judges have imposed death sentences for charges such as “endangering national unity” and “undermining public order and the security of society”. Amnesty International says that peaceful expressions of dissent, human rights advocacy and campaigning for political reform have also been treated as crimes against the state or as “terrorism”. When anti-discrimination protests intensified in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province in 2011–2012, the authorities cracked down on people suspected of participating in or supporting the demonstrations. Many protesters were arrested, including minors. The death penalty was used as a punishment. One of the most prominent cases in this category is that of Saud al-Faraj. The businessman was arrested in December 2019 on allegations of involvement in protests in Al-Qatif. He was sentenced to death in 2022 for participating in the 2011–2012 protests. His execution was carried out in June this year. The United Nations Working Group had previously deemed his detention unlawful and arbitrary. ESOHR has reported that another 49 people convicted over alleged peaceful expressions of dissent are now at risk of execution. They include Sheikh Salman al-Awda and Sheikh Hassan al-Maliki. Public prosecutors have been seeking the death penalty for them since 2018, but their trials remain unresolved to this day. This year’s figures: 83 of 108 executions not linked to murder In 2026, of the 108 executions documented by ESOHR, 84, or 77.7 per cent, were carried out on the basis of ta’zir. By category of offence, 71 executions (65.7 per cent) were for drug-related crimes, 25 (23 per cent) for murder, nine (around 8 per cent) in political and security-related cases, and three in other cases. In other words, 83 of the 108 executions were for offences unrelated to murder. ESOHR also reported that, before the executions were carried out, neither the organisation nor any other organisation had been able to obtain or document information about 91 of the 108 cases (84.2 per cent). In every case documented by human rights organisations, defendants have alleged that they were subjected to torture or ill-treatment during interrogation to extract confessions, which were subsequently admitted in court as evidence against them. According to these organisations, most death sentences and convictions in Saudi Arabia are based solely on coerced confessions. In the cases they examined or verified, allegations of torture were dismissed without any investigation. The allegations made by Saud al-Faraj are even more disturbing. He was repeatedly tortured because he refused to sign a false confession. He was beaten so severely that he had to be hospitalised, subjected to sexual violence, and his wife was threatened with gang rape. She was also forced to sign a statement against her husband under the threat of having their young child taken away. During his trial, he detailed the allegations of torture and submitted written complaints to the Specialised Criminal Court, the Public Prosecution, the Saudi Human Rights Commission and the crown prince himself. No investigation was initiated, and the court did not examine whether his confession was admissible. Jalal al-Labbad was sentenced to death for participating in protests in Al-Qatif when he was a minor. He was allegedly tortured through electric shocks, suffocation and beatings, and held in prolonged solitary confinement to force him to sign false statements. In several cases, including those of five young men sentenced to death for participating in protests during childhood, confessions extracted through torture were accepted as the sole evidence leading to conviction. Detention in isolation, cut off from the outside world, makes it easier to extract such coerced confessions. After his arrest on 2 December 2019, Saud al-Faraj spent more than 20 months in solitary confinement, without any contact with anyone outside. Jalal al-Labbad was held in solitary confinement for a total of nine months over two separate periods. Abdullah al-Derazi was cut off from the outside world for three months, and his family did not know where he was. Yusuf al-Manasif’s family was unable to visit him for five months after his arrest. Jawad Qureiris had no access to either a lawyer or his family during the investigation. Hassan Zaki al-Faraj spent three months in solitary confinement, while Farhat Abu al-Saud was held in isolation for four months. During his solitary confinement, Mohammed Labbad was beaten by several people at once with metal wires. He was kicked on various parts of his body, including his genitals, and suffocated by having a foot pressed against his throat. He was subjected to waterboarding and kept shackled at his hands and feet for prolonged periods. The United Nations Special Rapporteur on torture has repeatedly stated that no one should be convicted solely on the basis of a confession. According to the Working Group, coerced confessions taint the entire judicial process and seriously undermine the fundamental principles of a fair trial. Expatriates bear a disproportionate burden The burden of this judicial system does not fall equally on everyone. Of Saudi Arabia’s population of approximately 35.3 million, around 15.7 million are expatriates or foreign nationals, accounting for 44.4 per cent. Yet of the 122 executions carried out solely for drug-related offences in 2024, 92—or 75.4 per cent—involved foreign nationals. In 2025, at least 188 of the 240 executions for drug-related offences involved foreign nationals. In the first half of the current year, 59 of the 108 people executed—around 54 per cent—were foreign nationals. They included citizens of 17 countries, including Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia. In 2023, the United Nations Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination expressed particular concern over the “significant increase” in executions since 2023 and called for a moratorium on the death penalty. Two UN special rapporteurs also sent a joint letter to the Saudi government expressing concern over the potentially discriminatory application of the death penalty against foreign nationals convicted of drug-related offences. Death row prisoners awaiting execution Conditions in Saudi prisons, particularly for prisoners sentenced to death, are especially poor. They include overcrowding, unhygienic conditions and administrative neglect, including inadequate medical care. Before their executions, prisoners at Tabuk Prison were held in cramped, dirty cells with poor ventilation. On 18 February 2025, several prisoners began a hunger strike. They were protesting restrictions on contact with their families and degrading treatment, including being made to walk barefoot in handcuffs when being transferred for medical care. Saudi law contains no explicit provision requiring prisoners or their families to be notified in advance of an execution, nor does it guarantee the return of the body. In practice, families may learn that a loved one is about to be executed only 24 hours beforehand. Prisoners have interpreted the transfer of foreign inmates convicted of similar offences to isolated wards as a sign that executions are imminent. Amnesty International found that, in the cases of three people executed during the first half of 2025, their bodies were not returned to their families, and the locations of their graves were not disclosed. Even prisoners who believe their cases are still under review have been executed. Jordanian national Hussein Abu al-Khair had been asked by Saudi prison authorities to appoint a lawyer in preparation for a retrial. Shortly afterwards, he was executed. In June 2021, Abu al-Khair told his family that he had been informed that his “sentence had been suspended and was being reviewed by the Ministry of Interior under a royal directive, in connection with the pardon of some prisoners convicted of drug offences”. Although the sentences of several people around him were commuted, he remained in detention. In March 2023, he was executed without prior notice. The consequences of such assurances followed by sudden executions are not limited to the prisoners themselves. The same thing happened to the four Egyptian prisoners mentioned at the beginning of this report: after being assured that the crown prince had ordered their executions suspended, they were suddenly put to death. Such false assurances cause intense psychological anguish for prisoners and their families. Prisoners interviewed by ESOHR said they live in constant fear of execution. In recent months, they have witnessed death-row inmates being completely separated from others for a period of time, cut off from the outside world and then suddenly taken away for execution. UN recommendations and international obligations During a United Nations Universal Periodic Review in 2024, at least 35 recommendations were made concerning the death penalty in Saudi Arabia. Several countries called on the kingdom to move towards abolishing capital punishment by introducing a formal moratorium. Argentina recommended explicitly prohibiting the death penalty for offences committed by people under the age of 18. Amnesty International has called on Saudi Arabia to conduct an immediate, independent and transparent investigation into discrimination in the application of the death penalty. Under the Convention against Torture, Saudi Arabia is obliged to prevent torture and ensure that confessions obtained through torture are not admitted in legal proceedings. Yet the picture in the first six months of 2026 once again makes clear that Saudi Arabia continues to carry out executions at a rapid pace, without regard for its international obligations or publicly declared legal commitments. These include its commitments under the Convention against Torture and the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Despite growing international criticism and serious concerns over unfair trials, torture, discrimination and a lack of transparency, the country appears determined to maintain its position among the world’s leading executioners. Hussein Abu al-Khair’s sister told Amnesty International that her brother’s execution came after “nine years of torture”. He endured that suffering, as did his wife, children and the rest of his family. With his body never returned, the family had nothing with which to mourn him. After this long accounting of laws, courts and promised reforms, one question remains: in a country carrying out executions at record levels, does a person’s final news even reach their family in time? 1. article_text: Four new textbooks, two each for classes four and six, will be introduced in the next academic year. The two books for class four are “Bangladesh-er Sanskriti” (on Bangladesh’s culture), “Kheladhula” (on sports). The Class Six books are titled “Amar Karigori Shikkha” (on vocational studies) and “Anandamoy Shikkha” (literally translated: happy studies). The National Curriculum Coordination Committee (NCCC) approved the four books at separate meetings held on Sunday at the International Mother Language Institute in Segunbagicha, Dhaka. There are two NCCC committees: one for secondary education and the other for primary education. The primary education committee approved the two class four textbooks, while the secondary education committee approved the two class six books. However, the committees granted approval subject to necessary revisions, according to sources at the Ministry of Education. An official of the National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) told Prothom Alo that the authorities would revise the books in line with the recommendations and finalise them by Monday, today. Those present at Sunday’s meetings included Education and Primary and Mass Education Minister ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon, State Minister for Primary and Mass Education Bobby Hajjaj, Senior Secretary of the Secondary and Higher Education Division Abdul Khaleque, Chief Information Commissioner Nahreen Islam Khan, Prime Minister’s Press Secretary Saleh Shibli, and the Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Gias Uddin, among others. According to NCTB sources, the four textbooks will be compulsory for students in the two classes. However, schools will not hold annual examinations in these subjects; instead, teachers will assess students through continuous assessment. The total print run for the new books exceeds 15 million copies. On the day of approval, the authorities issued Notices of Award (NOAs) to the printers selected to produce the books. Sources familiar with the matter said one of the main objectives of the new Class six textbook “Amar Karigori Shikkha” is to encourage students to take an interest in vocational education. The book covers several chapters on Introduction to vocational education, technology around us and the new world, identifying problems and finding solutions, small initiatives and big possibilities, future careers and skills, green technology and sustainable living and glossary. The other new Class Six textbook, “Anandamoy Shikkha”, places emphasis on values. It is divided into several chapters on nutrition and healthy living, playing with technology, creating something new, staying lean and keeping our surroundings clean, days of celebration and living happily and spreading happiness. The new Class Four textbook “Bangladesh-er Sanskriti” will cover the concept of culture, its influence on personal life, national, religious and social festivals, Victory Day, 21 February and the importance of cultural practices. The other Class Four textbook on sports, focuses on eight sporting disciplines: football, cricket, badminton, kabaddi, chess, athletics, swimming and martial arts. Further changes to textbooks The National Curriculum and Textbook Board (NCTB) is introducing changes to textbooks for the 2027 academic year across various subjects, including history. These include adding information about the sectors and brigade forces of the Liberation War, biographies of all the Bir Sreshtho, the events of 7 November 1975, and former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia’s role in the mass uprising of 1990. The NCTB is also adding an article written by former President Ziaur Rahman, titled Memories of the War of Independence, to the Bangla textbook for classes nine and 10. In addition, the board is revising the accounts of the declaration of Bangladesh’s independence. The previous interim government also made changes to these accounts. As a result, textbooks produced under Awami League government, which was ousted during the July mass uprising, the revised textbooks prepared under the interim government, and the books being prepared under the current BNP government now present three different accounts of the declaration of independence. Controversy over textbook illustrations The Information and Communication Technology textbook for Class Six for the 2027 academic year included an illustration of weighing balance scale as a symbol of wisdom. However, following controversy over the image, the NCTB has decided to remove it before distributing the textbook to students. Notably, the current year’s textbooks did not feature the illustration of the scales. The board had added it specifically for next year’s edition. Following the controversy, the Ministry of Education transferred an NCTB official to Khagrachhari on Sunday. The official is a member of the education cadre. Meanwhile, the use of boat illustrations in several textbooks has also sparked controversy among some groups. However, several NCTB officials maintain that the illustrations match the subject matter and content of the books. The textbooks feature boats, rice harvesting and other relevant scenes to depict the enduring green landscape of rural Bengal. The authorities did not introduce these illustrations for the first time this year. They retained them during two rounds of textbook revisions under the interim government and again while revising the books for the next academic year under the current BNP government. title: How 'Maulana Diesel' became a last hope of Imran Khan
description: I never imagined that Maulana Fazlur Rehman would join those demanding the release of Imran Khan. A few years ago, the Maulana publicly branded Imran Khan a "Zionist agent," while Khan, at political rallies, mocked him as "Maulana Diesel." Today, the Maulana has become the last hope of Khan, who has been imprisoned for three years. Khan's popularity has failed to translate into a mass movement, partly because of fifth columnists within his own party. He knows that only the Maulana, the second most popular leader in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, can bring people onto the streets against the current government.
article_text: I never imagined that Maulana Fazlur Rehman would join those demanding the release of Imran Khan. A few years ago, the Maulana publicly branded Imran Khan a "Zionist agent," while Khan, at political rallies, mocked him as "Maulana Diesel." Today, the Maulana has become the last hope of Khan, who has been imprisoned for three years. Khan's popularity has failed to translate into a mass movement, partly because of fifth columnists within his own party. He knows that only the Maulana, the second most popular leader in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, can bring people onto the streets against the current government. I have known both men since 1988, when Pakistan's military ruler, General Zia-ul-Haq, dismissed Prime Minister Muhammad Khan Junejo on corruption charges. Junejo, of the Pakistan Muslim League, had been appointed by Zia himself after the non-party elections of 1985. Nawaz Sharif, then Chief Minister of Punjab, chose to side with Zia rather than stand by the prime minister of his own party. After removing Junejo, Zia decided to bring Imran Khan into the new government. Khan had retired from Test cricket in 1987 but returned at Zia's request. The general believed that Khan's presence would help repair his battered reputation. I was new to journalism in 1988 when I received a tip that Khan had been offered a ministry. When I contacted him to confirm it, he asked, "What do you think I should do?" I replied instantly: "Refuse." He said, "Fine, I will refuse, but don't make my refusal a news story, or it will create great difficulty for me." I could not sit on the story for long, and one day I published it. Khan was furious with me. Yet had he joined the government in 1988, he could not have led Pakistan to its Cricket World Cup victory in 1992. Around the same time, I interviewed a German scholar on the Silk Letter Movement (Tehreek-e-Resheemi Rumal). He told me that during the First World War, Deobandi scholars of the subcontinent, with the help of Afghanistan, Turkey and Germany, had devised the "Berlin Plan" to resist British rule. The Silk Letter Movement was part of that plan, and had it succeeded, India might have won its freedom in 1916. Maulana Fazlur Rehman read the interview and praised it warmly when we met in Lahore. He then sent me, through an associate, Maulana Syed Muhammad Miyan''s four-volume work Ulama-e-Hind Ka Shandar Mazi (The Glorious Past of the Ulema of India) so that I could learn more. That was the beginning of my respectful association with the Maulana. In 1990, Iraqi President Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and America sent forces to several Gulf countries to defend it. Pro-Saddam demonstrations erupted across Pakistan. One day, Shahid Sheikh, the sports reporter of Daily Jang Lahore, brought a statement from Imran Khan: "Whoever is not with Saddam is not a Muslim." It caused a stir, since the Pakistani government stood with Saudi Arabia rather than Saddam. For the first time, I heard Maulana Fazlur Rehman praise Imran Khan. My own opinion of Saddam was different, but it was clear that both men were critics of America. In 2002, another military ruler, General Pervez Musharraf, tried to give his unconstitutional government a constitutional veneer through elections. Imran Khan was his party's only member in the National Assembly. From Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, Asif Ali Zardari began efforts to make Maulana Fazlur Rehman prime minister, in opposition to Musharraf''s candidate, Mir Zafarullah Khan Jamali. Benazir Bhutto, in exile in Dubai, refused to support the Maulana under American pressure. Nawaz Sharif, in exile in Saudi Arabia, nominated him because he had no other option. Among those who voted for the Maulana were not only members of the Muslim League (N) but also Imran Khan. I remember that in those days, whenever some impudent person called the Maulana "Maulana Diesel," Khan would pick a fight with him. Maulana was opposition leader in the National Assembly those days.The nickname “Maulana Diesel” had been coined in 1995 by Nawaz Sharif''s supporters, when the Maulana was an ally of Benazir Bhutto, whose government was backing the Taliban in Afghanistan. Yet when this same Imran Khan became prime minister in 2018, he began using the same taunt at his rallies. The animosity grew so deep that in 2019, in an interview with me for Geo Television, the Maulana declared Khan a Zionist agent. That same year, the Maulana announced a long march against Khan's government. The then Army Chief, General Qamar Javed Bajwa, would summon journalists to Army House and tell them that the Maulana worked for British intelligence agency, MI6. Once I asked General Bajwa why he did not produce concrete evidence and take legal action. He promptly changed the subject. It was a curious contradiction: Bajwa extolled the benefits of friendship with Israel on one hand, while branding the Maulana a British agent on the other. The Muslim League (N) and the Pakistan Peoples Party then decided to use the Maulana against Khan. In 2020, the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM) was formed under his leadership, and a campaign against Khan''s government began. Khan set all the intelligence agencies and NAB to dig up evidence of the Maulana's corruption. ISI chief General Faiz Hameed personally planted fake stories against him with favoured journalists, and a media trial began. It had no effect on the Maulana. Intelligence agencies found nothing against Maulana. One former ISI official Major General Rtd Nusrat Naeem told me in those days that once he tried to buy the support of Maulana for General Musharraf and handed him over a bag full of money but Maulana refused to accept it. When I wrote that fact in a column supporters of Imran Khan started a compaign against me on social media. Meanwhile, Bajwa''s desire for friendship with Israel drove a wedge between him and Khan. Instead of granting Bajwa another extension as Army Chief , Khan decided to make General Faiz the Army Chief. In 2022, the opposition exploited the rift between the army chief and the prime minister and ousted Khan through a no-confidence motion. Out of power, Khan realized the Maulana''s importance and tried hard to forge an alliance with him, but failed. By then, the new ISI chief, General Nadeem Anjum, had driven the Muslim League (N) and the PPP away from the Maulana. This was the same Maulana who, in 2010, had persuaded ulema(religious scholars) from across the country at Jamia Ashrafia Lahore to sign a unanimous declaration against terrorism. Now he was being labelled a supporter of terrorists. After that declaration, he survived back-to-back suicide attacks in Swabi, Charsadda and Quetta, yet never abandoned his stand against militancy in politics. That was his great contribution to Pakistan''s democratic process. It is true that both Khan and Maulana favoured talks with the Taliban government in Afghanistan, but even so, the Maulana avoided becoming Khan''s political ally. A few weeks before the 2024 elections, Khan sent a message from jail: "Set all the conditions you want for an alliance, and I will endorse them blindly." The Maulana politely declined. He told me one day, "I refused to sign an agreement with Imran Khan because I once declared him a Zionist agent." The mistrust between them ran deep. In the end, it was the Shehbaz Sharif government's missteps that brought them together. Now Khan is behind the bars. His chief minister and many members of the parliament are in the custody of security agencies but Maulana is raising a strong voice against the authoritarian tactics of Shehbaz Sharif government. The Maulana says that Khan has been jailed along with all the women of his family, and that governor's rule has been imposed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. "In these circumstances," he says, "we have no option but to resist oppression." These days, social media is flooded with government sponsored fake videos and baseless allegations against the Maulana, and he is being threatened with arrest. He has been arrested eleven times in his political life and now he is ready for a twelfth arrest.The credit for bringing the Maulana and Khan closer goes to Shehbaz Sharif. Just as Khan appreciated the Maulana's importance only after losing power, the Muslim League (N) too will remember him only after losing power. But perhaps the Maulana will not fall into their trap again. # Hamid Mir is a Pakistani journalist who works for Geo News @HamidMirPAK

title: Bangladesh's cyber security challenge: Do we know what is exposed?
description: In Bangladesh, many of us now depend on digital services throughout the day without thinking much about the systems behind them.
