article_text: In Bangladesh, many of us now depend on digital services throughout the day without thinking much about the systems behind them. We send money through mobile financial services, check bank accounts, pay bills, use government services and log in to university or office systems. The scale is large. Bangladesh Bank data show that mobile financial services handled transactions worth more than Tk 2.16 lakh crore in July 2026, up 45.73 per cent from the same month a year earlier. All of this depends on digital infrastructure that has to remain connected and available. That raises a question: does the organisation providing the service know exactly what parts of its own infrastructure can be seen from the internet? Most organisations have a fairly good idea of what sits inside their network. What someone outside can see is harder to answer. Systems are added, moved, upgraded and replaced all the time. Some stay online long after the job they were built for has ended. So over time, what is visible from outside can become much bigger than the list everyone thinks they are protecting. I spent nearly two decades in network and cyber security in Bangladesh's banking sector. Most of that work was protecting systems we already knew about: networks, firewalls, servers and applications. Today that is not enough. We also have to look at an organisation the way an outsider sees it and ask: what can actually be seen from the internet? This matters more every year. Government offices, banks, mobile financial services, telecom operators, educational institutions, hospitals and businesses all depend on connected systems. Firewalls and monitoring are still essential. But they work best when an organisation knows what it is putting in front of the world in the first place. That is where attack surface mapping helps. What is an attack surface? Think of a house. The owner knows the front door and locks it every night. But what about the back gate, the old window in the storeroom, the side door nobody has used for years? An attacker only needs one of them. An attack surface is the same idea for computer systems. It is everything that can be seen or reached from the internet: a public website, a remote-access service, a mail server, a cloud application, or an old system that nobody uses much anymore but is still switched on. Attack surface mapping means finding all of these and building an honest picture of what an outsider can see. That includes domain names, IP addresses, open services and the software they run. Being visible does not mean being unsafe. An exposed system is not necessarily weak, and not every weakness gets used by an attacker. The value of mapping is that it gives the security team a better place to start. It matters because things keep changing. New applications go live, cloud services are added, systems are moved and old ones stay longer than planned. In a big organisation, what is visible from outside can change faster than the internal list of assets. Mapping does not replace vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, audits or monitoring. It makes them more focused. Take penetration testing. Testers are normally given an agreed list of systems to test, and anything outside the list is left alone. That is right, because testing must be controlled and authorised. But if a system facing the internet never made it into the inventory, it may never make it into the test either. Cybersecurity threat spreads worldwide, affecting Bangladesh too Mapping comes first. It shows what is really visible, so testing can focus on the right systems. Red-team exercises go a step further. They use realistic attack scenarios to check whether weaknesses can be used, and also whether the organisation can notice and respond to an attack. Bangladesh is not starting from zero Bangladesh already has cyber security institutions, experienced professionals and ongoing work. BGD e-GOV CIRT, under the Bangladesh Computer Council, is the country's national cyber incident response body and helps protect important digital infrastructure. Bangladesh Bank has maintained ICT security requirements for the financial sector for years. More recently, it issued BRPD-2 Circular No. 02 on 29 March 2026, introducing the Cybersecurity Framework, Version 1.0 (2026). Regulated financial institutions must comply by 31 December 2026. Websites shut down worldwide amid fears of cyberattacks: How prepared is Bangladesh? So the point is not that Bangladesh has no cyber security controls. That would be unfair and wrong. The point is that mapping adds one more layer of visibility to the work already being done. Vulnerability assessment, monitoring, risk management and policy all work better when everyone has a clearer picture of what is exposed. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the problem Once an organisation knows what is exposed, the next step is to look for weaknesses: old or unpatched software, wrong settings, known security flaws. A scan of a large environment can return hundreds or even thousands of findings. That sounds useful. But a long list does not tell the team what to fix first. That is where the real work begins. No organisation has unlimited people, time or downtime. Fixes need testing. Important systems cannot always be taken offline. Some updates depend on the vendor. Even a routine fix in a critical system may need careful planning. So the number of weaknesses tells us very little. A few serious ones on an exposed, important system may deserve far more attention than a long list of minor ones somewhere else. Good security work is not about chasing the biggest number in a report. It is about knowing what matters most. Penetration testing helps when a team needs to be sure. Can this weakness really be used? How much damage could it do? Would our existing controls stop an attacker? Deciding what needs attention first Three tools help here: CVSS, EPSS and KEV. CVSS, the Common Vulnerability Scoring System, gives a numerical score for the technical severity of a weakness, commonly grouped as low, medium, high or critical. But severity is only part of the story. A high score tells us a weakness could do serious damage. It does not tell us how likely attackers are to use it, or how important the affected system is to the organisation. Cyberattack fears: Janata Bank, Bengal Commercial Bank websites go offline EPSS, the Exploit Prediction Scoring System, estimates how likely it is that a known weakness will be exploited in the near future. In simple terms, CVSS shows how bad it could be. EPSS shows how likely it is to happen. KEV, the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, lists weaknesses that attackers have already used in real attacks. No single one of these is enough. The team still has to ask whether the system is open to the internet, how important it is, what service depends on it and what would happen if it were compromised. Only then does a list of weaknesses turn into a real decision. Why this matters for Bangladesh This is not a problem unique to Bangladesh. Every organisation has limits on how much it can fix at once. But it matters a great deal for a country that depends more on digital services every year. A risk-based approach focuses on weaknesses that are both serious and likely to be used. Mapping adds one more question: can the affected system actually be reached from the internet? Together, these give a far better basis for deciding what to fix first than simply counting weaknesses. There is value beyond one organisation too. If this information is handled responsibly, without exposing sensitive details, it can show wider patterns: technologies that keep appearing, the same kinds of exposure repeating, or places where more training and capacity are needed. Bangladesh already has practitioners, researchers, regulators and national institutions working on these issues. Sharing technical information better among them can lead to better decisions. The benefit reaches beyond security teams. Managers get a clearer view of external risk and where to invest. Auditors can compare what is written in the records with what the outside world can really see. And the public has a stake. A cyber incident in a bank can affect customers and financial services. In a hospital, it can affect patients. An attack on government systems can disrupt public services. A problem at a telecom operator can affect every organisation that depends on its network. A weakness inside one organisation can therefore hurt people far beyond it. Cyber security will always need firewalls, monitoring, skilled people, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, red-team exercises where needed and incident response. Attack surface mapping does not replace any of them. Its value is different. It answers a question that is easy to overlook: what is actually exposed? CVSS, EPSS and KEV are useful too, but only alongside the organisation's own reality. Severity matters. Likelihood matters. Known exploitation matters. So does how important the system is. As Bangladesh's digital transformation continues, keeping track of what is visible from outside can strengthen the work already being done by institutions, regulators, practitioners and researchers. The goal is not the longest possible list of weaknesses. It is to understand what is exposed, what really matters and what to fix first. So alongside asking whether our organisations have policies, firewalls and vulnerability management programmes, there is one more question worth asking regularly: Do we actually know what is exposed? Knowing the answer is an important step towards protecting what matters most. * SM Abdul Wadud is pursuing a Master of Cyber Security at the University of Waikato, New Zealand. He has nearly 20 years of professional experience in network and cyber security in Bangladesh's banking sector.

title: Madrasah head accused of kidnapping student after she rejects his romantic proposal
description: The director and headteacher of a madrasah in Gazipur’s Sadar upazila have been accused of kidnapping a Class Eight student. The girl’s father filed a case against five people at Joydebpur Police Station on Sunday night.
article_text: The director and headteacher of a madrasah in Gazipur’s Sadar upazila have been accused of kidnapping a Class Eight student. The girl’s father filed a case against five people at Joydebpur Police Station on Sunday night. The prime accused is Ariful Islam, 29, who runs two madrasahs in the Joydebpur police station area and serves as their headteacher. The other accused are his brother, Sharif Mia, 35; their father, Selim Mia, 55; their mother, Rahima Khatun, 40; and a man named Delwar Hossain, 45. Madrasah teacher beaten, handed over to police over alleged rape of child According to the case statement, all the accused are from Char Bawla village in Mymensingh Sadar upazila. The student was in Class Eight at a girls’ madrasah run by Ariful Islam. He allegedly made romantic advances towards her and harassed her in various ways. When she refused his advances, he threatened to kidnap her. After the student told her family about the matter, they asked Ariful to stop such behaviour. Angered by this, he allegedly continued to intimidate and threaten them. The case statement says that on the morning of 10 October, after the student arrived at the madrasah, Ariful allegedly took her away by force with the help of his associates. Madrasah principal arrested over alleged rape of student After learning about the incident through various sources, the girl’s father searched several possible locations. Unable to find his daughter, he eventually filed a case with the police. The girl’s father said his daughter went missing after leaving for the madrasah, as she did every day, at around 7:30 am. He later learned that the accused teacher, Ariful Islam, had allegedly kidnapped her with the help of others. Joydebpur Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Al Mamun confirmed the case and said police were conducting operations to rescue the student and arrest the accused.

article_text: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived in Tokyo Monday morning (local time) on a four-day official visit at the invitation of his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, aiming to deepen bilateral ties, attract investment and expand trade and development cooperation. A Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Zubaida Rahman, and members of his entourage landed at Narita International Airport at 9:07 am local time. The prime minister was received at the airport by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Yasutaka Nakasone. A motorcade then escorted him to Tokyo’s Imperial Hotel, where he will stay during his visit. Japan to invest Tk 774.7 billion in Bangladesh Prime Minister’s Adviser for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology and Science and Technology Rehan Asif Asad, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister for Foreign Employment in the Asia-Pacific region Md Shakirul Islam Khan, and senior officials of the Bangladesh Embassy in Tokyo were also present. Earlier, the prime minister left Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka early today Bangladesh time for Japan aboard a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight, accompanied by a small delegation. Tarique Rahman is scheduled to hold a high-level bilateral talk with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi at her office on 27 October, followed by a joint press announcement and a luncheon hosted by the Japanese premier, according to the Prime Minister’s press wing. During the four-day visit, the prime minister will also meet Japanese government officials, development institutions and business leaders, visit industrial and energy facilities, and deliver the keynote address at the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum. The premier's visit is expected to deepen the existing strategic partnership, attract fresh Japanese investment, expand trade and accelerate ongoing development projects, Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam told journalists at a curtain-raiser media briefing at the Foreign Ministry on 20 October. Discussions will focus on the effective implementation of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, expanding access for Bangladeshi products to the Japanese market and strengthening business engagement. What Bangladesh can gain from PM's Japan visit The two sides will also explore wider cooperation in renewable energy, agriculture, science and technology, digital transformation, skills development and human resource development. His tentative programme includes engagements with the Japan-Bangladesh Parliamentary Friendship League and the chairman of the Japan-Bangladesh Committee for Commercial and Economic Cooperation. Meetings are also being planned with the president of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO) and the chairman of the Sasakawa Peace Foundation, said the foreign secretary. The proposed itinerary includes visits to an LNG terminal and power plant in Futtsu City, Chiba, the headquarters of UNIQLO and a Toyota factory in Nagoya. The foreign secretary said the two sides were discussing draft memoranda of understanding and cooperation agreements covering agriculture, fisheries, human resource development, skills enhancement, civil aviation, trade, environmental conservation and local government modernisation. "We hope that many of these MoUs will be signed during the visit," he said. Around eight MoUs are under discussion, of which three to four could be signed during the visit. Separate agreements are also being pursued in education and human resource development. Detailed discussions are planned on Japanese support for establishing factories in Bangladesh, generating employment and developing human resources in line with the prime minister's priorities. PM’s Japan visit: Reducing metro rail costs, loan interest rates likely to be discussed The two sides are also expected to discuss regional and international peace and stability, a sustainable and peaceful solution to the Rohingya crisis, stronger cooperation in addressing the energy crisis and efforts to end international conflicts. The visit follows the prime minister's participation in an online meeting in April at the invitation of the Japanese premier, during which Bangladesh welcomed a Japan-led initiative to address energy challenges across Asia. Japan has been a major development partner of Bangladesh since the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1972. Japanese assistance has supported major infrastructure projects, including the Dhaka metro rail, the third terminal of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport and infrastructure development in Matarbari.

title: Journalist murdered in Netrokona: Alif was targeted by criminals while investigating border crime
description: Alif was from Sunai village in Pogla Union, Kalmakanda Upazila, Netrokona. His in-laws lived in Telunjia village in Birishiri Union, Durgapur Upazila. A retired member of the armed forces, Alif worked as the Netrokona correspondent for the IP television channel Ruposhi Bangla. He also ran a Facebook page called Detective Article. Through his reporting, Alif exposed smuggling, drug trafficking, arms-related activities and other wrongdoing along the border. He regularly published photographs and videos. According to the police and his family, there had already been two attempts on his life. Fearing for his safety, he had moved to his in-laws’ house. It was there that gunmen eventually killed him. He sustained six bullet wounds to the head, neck and chest.
article_text: A narrow, brick-paved road leads from the local highway into the village. A three-minute walk along it brings us to Robin Rangsa’s small shop, where he sells tea, biscuits and basic groceries. Just a short distance from the shop, journalist Lutfozzaman Alif Fakir, 44, was shot dead at around 8:30 pm on 15 October. Robin was at the shop when the shooting took place. Last Friday, he recounted the incident to us. Robin said Alif had stopped by at around 8:00 pm that night and bought six cigarettes. He sat at a table in the shop and smoked one before heading to his in-laws’ house nearby. Alif had been living there for about two years. In his haste to leave, he accidentally left his mobile phone on the table. According to Robin, two other customers arrived and bought cigarettes while Alif was away. One was wearing a lungi, the other three-quarter-length trousers. A short while later, Alif returned to collect his phone and set off for his in-laws’ house again. Almost immediately after he left the shop, Robin heard gunshots. Journalist shot dead in Netrokona Robin was washing tea cups when he heard the gunshots. He looked up and saw Alif lying on the ground, with the two men still at the scene. Terrified, Robin retreated into his home behind the shop. Asked whether he recognised the two men, Robin said he did not. He had never seen them before. Alif was from Sunai village in Pogla Union, Kalmakanda Upazila, Netrokona. His in-laws lived in Telunjia village in Birishiri Union, Durgapur Upazila. A retired member of the armed forces, Alif worked as the Netrokona correspondent for the IP television channel Ruposhi Bangla. He also ran a Facebook page called Detective Article. Through his reporting, Alif exposed smuggling, drug trafficking, arms-related activities and other wrongdoing along the border. He regularly published photographs and videos. According to the police and his family, there had already been two attempts on his life. Fearing for his safety, he had moved to his in-laws’ house. It was there that gunmen eventually killed him. He sustained six bullet wounds to the head, neck and chest. The day after the murder, his wife, Khadija, filed a case against seven to eight unidentified people. Police say Tajul Islam, 48, and Shamim Ahmed, 32, also known as “Shooter Shamim”, are among the leading suspects. The two men maintain separate networks of associates involved in illegal border trade, though they sometimes work together. Investigators are examining whether they helped plan or finance Alif’s murder and whether they had links to the attackers. Alif’s in-laws’ house stands about 300 yards from Robin’s shop. After speaking with Robin, we headed there. Alif had lived in a small hut with tin-sheet walls. Among the old furniture and household belongings, a pair of blue trainers stood out. They had faded with years of use. His shirt, denim trousers and blazer had also lost much of their original colour. Alif’s wife, Khadija Akter, belongs to the Garo community. The two had been in a romantic relationship before their marriage. She converted to Islam when they married; her parents had named her Anondita Sangma. We found Khadija in the room where she had lived with Alif and their two young children. She told Prothom Alo that she initially did not realise the sound she heard was gunfire. She thought someone had set off firecrackers. Then a neighbour told her that Alif had been shot, and she rushed to the scene. ‘Feed the children and put them to sleep, I’ll be a little late’ Khadija said she lifted Alif’s head onto her lap and checked for a heartbeat. Having studied nursing, she understood that her husband was dead. She remained there, sitting beside him, until the police arrived some time later. As she spoke, Khadija wept. She said the family had planned to move to Dhaka the following month, November. Her mother had even taken out a loan of Tk 40,000 to help them make the move. But Alif died before they could carry out their plans. Kalmakanda and Durgapur are neighbouring upazilas in Netrokona, both bordering India’s Meghalaya state. Smuggling across the border involves a wide range of goods, including drugs, sugar, cosmetics, blankets, cattle, machinery parts and firearms. According to police and local sources, Shamim Ahmed controls part of the smuggling trade along the Durgapur border. Tajul, meanwhile, leads a criminal gang accused of extortion, smuggling and other offences. Both men have been accused of involvement in a range of crimes, including murder, attempted murder, arms offences, drug trafficking, explosives-related offences, kidnapping, extortion, robbery and theft. At least 25 cases have been identified against Shamim, filed at Durgapur Police Station between 2014 and 2026. Eleven involve charges of attempted murder, and 19 cases remain pending. Shamim has also been accused in two murder cases. On 8 October, 2022, Subrata Sangma, a former chairman of Kullagora Union Parishad in Durgapur, was killed. His sister filed a case naming Shamim as the main accused. On 4 February, 2024, Shamim was again named as the main accused in the murder of Mojibur Rahman, known as “Dao Mojibur”, from Naljora village in Birishiri Union. The case was filed by Mojibur’s son. At least 13 cases have been identified against Tajul. Ten were filed at Durgapur Police Station, while one each was filed at Kalmakanda Police Station, Netrokona Sadar Police Station and Darus Salam Police Station in Dhaka. The cases date from 2006 to 2022. Three involve allegations of attempted murder, and four include charges under the Arms Act. Alif had reported on both Shamim and Tajul on several occasions. At least five people who knew him and were familiar with his work told Prothom Alo that he was determined to expose crime and wrongdoing on Facebook. Threats and pressure were not enough to make him take down his posts. His Facebook page was one of his main reporting platforms. Khadija said Alif had gathered information about Tajul’s smuggling activities and weapons and passed it on to the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). RAB arrested Tajul about four years ago. Khandaker Shaker Ahmed, officer-in-charge (OC) of Durgapur Police Station, offered an account that partly supported Khadija’s statement. Speaking to Prothom Alo at his office last Friday, he said Alif had collected information about Tajul’s activities and published photographs and videos of his home and property on Facebook. Tajul believed Alif had also informed law enforcement agencies about the weapons he possessed. The resentment this created had led to an earlier attack on Alif, the OC said. Shamim, too, had featured in Alif’s reporting. According to sources involved in the investigation, about a week before the murder, Alif posted a video that allegedly showed Shamim using yaba. Investigators are looking into whether the video prompted any fresh threats. On 14 October, the day before his killing, Alif posted a brief message on his Detective Article page announcing that he would reveal evidence about a “godfather” of crime the following day. At 7:28 pm on 15 October, the same page published a 41-second video alleging that a man named Babul had played a role in resettling Rohingya people in Netrokona. Investigators are examining whether either of these posts had a direct connection to the murder. Threats, Cases, Arrests and Allegations of Torture According to his family, efforts to silence Alif went beyond threats. Cases were filed against him, and he was allegedly beaten after being arrested. Alif’s wife, Khadija, said that on 19 March 2024, Alif posted on Facebook about then Superintendent of Police Faiz Ahmed. He had planned to publish further information the following day. But the next day, men identifying themselves as members of the Detective Branch (DB) took him away. The family alleged that police beat Alif so severely that he had to be taken to hospital. When he was brought before a court, he was still unable to walk properly. Faiz Ahmed, who is currently posted in Khulna, told Prothom Alo by phone on Saturday that the incident had not unfolded as described. He said Alif had written about many people, including superintendents of police, on numerous occasions—not just that day. According to Faiz, Alif was arrested in connection with a rape case. After Alif was detained, two cases were filed against him: one for extortion and another for rape. Documents obtained by Prothom Alo show that the case under the Women and Children Repression Prevention Act was filed at Kalmakanda Police Station on 5 April 2024. After completing its investigation, police submitted a final report on 11 April 2025, indicating that they had found no evidence to substantiate the allegation. Alif’s wife, Khadija, said the case had been filed to harass him. She also said that after Alif wrote about smuggling along the border, Oli Ahmed, a local leader of the now-banned Awami League, filed an extortion case against him. ‘Police Officer Killed After Being Mistaken for Alif’ In one of the earlier attempts to kill Alif, a police sub-inspector lost his life. The officer, Mohammad Shafiqul Islam, was hacked to death on 9 January 2025 in the Panmahal area of Durgapur Municipality. A subsequent police investigation found that the attackers had been targeting Alif. Mohammad Imdadul Bashar, an inspector with the Netrokona office of the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) and the case’s investigating officer, told Prothom Alo that two arrested suspects, Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo, 21, and Mohammad Baki Billah, gave confessional statements in court. They said they had killed Shafiqul by mistake while attempting to kill Alif. According to their statements, Tajul had ordered the attack. Apurbo and Baki Billah were currently out on bail. Police believe they were involved in the attack on Alif. Nearly 10 months later, on 10 November 2025, Alif was seriously injured when attackers struck him with machetes near the Teribazar ferry terminal on the Someshwari River. He survived. He filed a case naming two suspects: Samiul Haque, alias Sourav, and Mohammad Imon Mia. Both are out on bail. A charge sheet was submitted in September. Police suspect that they also took part in the latest attack. At a meeting between journalists and the district superintendent of police on 30 November 2025, Alif spoke about the danger he faced, saying, “If I go out, they’ll shoot me.” Sources involved in the investigation now say they have found links between the earlier attacks and the latest killing. Six Names from an Old List Durgapur Police Station maintains a list of 22 suspected criminals. Sources involved in the investigation say evidence has so far emerged linking six people on that list to Alif’s murder: Tajul Islam; Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo; Mohammad Ashikur Rahman, alias Prangan, 19; Mohammad Sabbir Hossain, 20; Baki Billah, 20; and Samiul Haque, alias Sourav. Four of the six were allegedly involved in earlier attacks. According to police sources, investigators have also found links between people close to Shamim and Tajul’s associates. They said they had obtained information suggesting that Tajul helped plan the killing while Shamim provided financial support. Two people have been arrested in the Alif murder case: Sajibul Islam, alias Apurbo, and Ashikur Rahman, alias Prangan. Police say Apurbo is an associate of Tajul, while Prangan is close to Shamim and is the son of Shamim’s cousin. Prangan was arrested by SRB-14, the former RAB. Sources involved in the investigation said Prangan contacted Shamim after the shooting to find out whether Alif had died. Officer-in-Charge Khondaker Shaker Ahmed said Imon was riding Tajul’s motorcycle on the evening of Alif’s murder. Another associate, Sourav, was also present. Investigators are examining each person’s whereabouts and role. The source of the weapon is another key part of the investigation. According to police, the bullets used in Alif’s murder were 9mm rounds. Shamim’s Brother Is a Union Parishad Chairman Since Alif’s murder, Shamim and his associates have gone into hiding. Shamim is the half-brother of Abdul Awal, general secretary of the Durgapur upazila unit of the BNP and chairman of Kullagora Union Parishad. According to local sources, Shamim was previously known as a follower of the late Manu Majumder, a former Awami League member of parliament. Shamim could not be reached for comment on the allegations. His half-brother, Abdul Awal, said political opponents were trying to tarnish Shamim’s reputation. Asked why Shamim and other family members were being linked to smuggling along the border, Abdul Awal said, “Others are involved in these activities, but our names get dragged into it.” Tajul lives in Bagichapara, within Durgapur Municipality. He and his associates have gone into hiding. How Far Has the Investigation Progressed? Netrokona Superintendent of Police Mohammad Tarikul Islam told Prothom Alo on Saturday, “The group of killers is more or less clear. We are investigating the involvement of those who control the group. Two people have been arrested, and they are being questioned. We expect to deliver results soon.” A special committee led by an additional superintendent of police has been formed to investigate Alif’s murder. Other investigative agencies have also been brought in. Alif’s mobile phone has been sent to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) for forensic examination. Mohammad Zahidul Hasan, deputy inspector general (DIG) of police for the Mymensingh Range, told Prothom Alo that the investigation had made considerable progress and that details would be disclosed soon. ‘There Couldn’t Be a Better Person’ The Durgapur and Kalmakanda upazilas of Netrokona are home to several Indigenous communities, including the Garo and Hajong. Most residents of Telunjia village in Birishiri Union, Durgapur—the village where Alif’s in-laws live—belong to the Garo community. Alif’s relatives on his wife’s side said he got along well with everyone. Members of the family and community considered him one of their own. Alif’s mother-in-law, Shila Sangma, and his late father-in-law, Philip Rema, had three daughters and one son. Alif’s wife is the eldest daughter. Shila used to call Alif “Babu”. She told Prothom Alo, “He was like my own son. There couldn’t be a better person.” After the July mass uprising, criminals operating along the Durgapur border switched political allegiances, but the criminal activities continued. Alif was attacked twice last year while reporting on those activities. In the third attack, he was shot six times and killed. Questions have now been raised about what the police did to protect him. Haider Jahan Chowdhury, convener of the voluntary organisation Janaudyog and former district commander of the Muktijoddha (Freedom Fighters) Unit in Netrokona, told Prothom Alo, “We are stunned by the way journalist Alif was shot dead. Unless those responsible are identified quickly, brought to justice and given exemplary punishment, such incidents will continue to happen.”

title: Brazil's Lula defies odds to clinch poll victory against Bolsonaro
description: Brazil's leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. With Lula's victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries -- such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru -- all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term. According to official results, he won 51.7 per cent of the votes to 48.2 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls.
article_text: Brazil's leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva pulled off a dramatic comeback on Sunday as he clinched election victory against right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who trounced him in the first round. With Lula's victory, Brazil staved off a conservative wave that has seen numerous countries -- such as Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru -- all shift right, backed by US President Donald Trump. The leftist icon, who turns 81 on Tuesday, defied all projections to win an unprecedented fourth term. According to official results, he won 51.7 per cent of the votes to 48.2 per cent for Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, who had entered election day confident with his lead in the polls. Bolsonaro clan wins big in multiple Brazil polls Since the first direct election following the end of Brazil's dictatorship in 1989, no candidate who lost the first round had gone on to win the second. Fireworks and vuvuzelas rang out in Rio de Janeiro, while thousands of people dressed in red, the color of Lula's Workers' Party, streamed into the streets of Sao Paulo to celebrate. In a video posted to social media, the president appeared jumping for joy,wearing red, star-shaped glasses, at a hotel in Sao Paulo, where he is scheduled to speak to the press later. Flavio Bolsonaro, who is in Brasilia, has yet to react. In Cinelandia Square, in the heart of Rio, Lula's supporters were moved to tears. Julio Canelo, 42, a lawyer hailed a victory for "the entire democratic spectrum." "It was the result of the people mobilizing, in the streets and online," he told AFP. The left swung into action with massive rallies after the first-round defeat, declaring "Never Again Bolsonaro" and revamping a lacklustre social media strategy. The abstention rate decreased from the first round, falling from 21 per cent to 19 per cent. A bitter campaign marred by scandals and mudslinging laid bare the deep divisions that have remained in the country of over 200 million people over the past decade. Lula heads into a fourth term with a country divided, with almost half of the nation having rejected him, desperate for change. Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, pitched himself as more moderate and jovial than his father and managed to galvanize conservatives as well as less ideological voters fed up with crime, the high cost of living and a sense of stagnation. "We're in a deep hole, things are dire. People can barely afford to eat -- buying meat is out of the question," said Tereza Cristina Ramos, a 68-year-old retiree, who voted in Rio de Janeiro. After a campaign marred by scandal and mud-slinging, Sunday's vote plunged into chaos after a last-minute Supreme Court ruling extending voting by two hours, at the request of Lula who said buses had been pulled from circulation in various cities, barring citizens from voting. Lula's re-election marks another remarkable comeback for the man who grew up dirt poor in the northeast, in a family of illiterate farmers. He rose to the presidency as a working-class hero, taking office for the first time in 2003. He was re-elected in 2006. Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic return to office in 2022 elections after a corruption scandal saw him jailed for over 18 months. The charges, annulled on procedural grounds, have continued to haunt him. In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, and lifted millions out of hunger, but many voters who turned to Flavio Bolsonaro felt gloomy about their economic situation and fed up with crime. After a campaign marked by fearmongering on both sides -- many voters reported choosing what they considered the lesser evil. Already one of the world's oldest leaders, Lula will be 85 by the end of his new term in 2030. He will thus have spent 16 years in power, following his first stint as president from 2003 through 2010. Lula is also facing a hostile Congress dominated by the right. His options are constrained by the economic outlook, with growth expected to slow. He has also come under renewed pressure to confront rampant security problems in a country plagued by criminal factions that sow terror in working-class neighborhoods. The president's campaign leaned heavily on the theme of sovereignty in the face of commercial and diplomatic pressure from Trump's United States. Voters must "choose a country where the flag is respected," he said, his raspy voice more hoarse than ever after a tireless campaign. He accused his rival of wanting to "govern with the American flag."

title: Women constitute 63pc of medical students
description: Women now make up nearly 63 per cent of students in Bangladesh’s public and private medical colleges, about 61 per cent in dental colleges, and around 90 per cent in nursing and midwifery programmes. Female MBBS graduates also outnumber men. However, women remain slightly underrepresented among physicians in government service and BCS recruitment, despite being a majority of applicants. Experts attribute the education trend to academic merit and family support, while citing workplace barriers and concentration in specialties such as obstetrics and gynaecology as reasons for professional disparities.
article_text: Female enrolment in medical education has risen significantly across Bangladesh. Women currently account for nearly 63 per cent of all students pursuing degrees in public and private medical colleges. Female students also outnumber their male counterparts in dental education, while in nursing and midwifery programmes, women represent approximately 90 per cent of total enrolments. However, the proportion of female physicians in the professional sphere, particularly in government jobs, remains comparatively lower. The trend of advancement of women observed at the primary, secondary, and higher secondary levels is visibly mirrored in medical education. Nevertheless, this continuity is not uniformly maintained across the university sector. Outside the affiliated colleges of the National University, the proportion of female students in public and private universities remains below 40 per cent. The predominance of female students in medical colleges has been evident for the past eight to 10 years. The number of female graduates passing the MBBS examinations also exceeds that of males. Consequently, female participation among newly qualifying physicians entering the workforce is expanding at a higher rate than previously recorded. The report titled Bangladesh Education Statistics 2025, published by the Bangladesh Bureau of Educational Information and Statistics (BANBEIS), outlines the trajectory of women's progress in medical education alongside general education metrics. According to the report, in 2025, a total of 51,313 students were enrolled across 109 public and private medical colleges nationwide (with two additional colleges receiving approval subsequently). Of these students, 62.79 per cent were female. In the 37 public medical colleges, women comprised 61.57 per cent of the total student body. Meanwhile, in the 72 private medical colleges, the proportion of female students stood at 63.60 per cent. Medical student crisis: No compromise with quality of education Medical colleges impart training through the MBBS degree programme. The clear female majority in this course indicates that women now constitute a substantial proportion of those on the path to becoming medical professionals. The leading position of female students is evident across both public and private institutions. However, in the professional workforce, specifically in the government jobs, female physicians continue to lag behind slightly. In the 39th (Special) BCS examination, the Public Service Commission (PSC) recommended 6,792 physicians for appointment. Among those recommended, 53 per cent were male and 47 per cent female, despite women comprising over 56 per cent of the total applicant pool. A similar pattern emerged in the 42nd (Special) BCS examination, where 4,000 physicians were recommended for recruitment. Of these, approximately 51 per cent were male and 49 per cent female, while women accounted for nearly 56 per cent of the applicants. Women lead in dentistry and nursing as well Female representation is dominant not only in MBBS programmes but also across other health-related academic disciplines. According to Education Statistics 2025, nearly 7,500 students are currently enrolled across the country's 35 dental colleges and dental units, of whom 60.85 per cent are female. Female participation is even higher in nursing and midwifery education. Bangladesh houses 475 nursing and midwifery colleges and institutes, with a combined student body of approximately 40,000. Nearly 90 per cent of them are female. Physicians, dental surgeons, nurses, and midwives all play vital roles in forming a skilled healthcare workforce across various tiers of service delivery. However, sector experts note that alongside female numerical superiority in education, it is equally crucial to assess the extent to which their workforce participation, professional career progression, and leadership opportunities are advancing. Women's advancement in Bangladesh vs. gender backlash The trend of female predominance in medical education is not entirely new. Statistics from the Directorate General of Health Education (DGHE) on medical admissions and MBBS pass rates between 2009 and 2018 corroborate this pattern. According to the data, a total of 48,777 domestic students cleared the MBBS examinations over that decade, of whom 26,901 were female, representing roughly 55 per cent of all successful graduates. Academic merit, family encouragement, and educational progress Education professionals attribute the growing representation of women in medical education to several major factors. Female participation has expanded at the primary, secondary, and higher secondary levels, where the proportion of female students currently exceeds 50 per cent. Girls also outperform boys in achieving GPA-5, the highest performance benchmark in public examinations. As a result, female participation in the competitive admission exams for higher education continues to grow. At the same time, according to them, the strong interest of high-achieving female students in pursuing a medical career, alongside encouraging family support, plays a pivotal role. Socioeconomic background, access to education, career preferences, and success in admission examinations further contribute to this trend. Another significant facet of female participation in medical education is their professional field of choice. Researchers from the BRAC James P Grant School of Public Health and icddr,b (International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research, Bangladesh) analysed data from 34,697 physicians registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (BMDC) between 2006 and 2015. Women lag behind in higher education and employment The analysis revealed that among registered physicians, 48 per cent were male and 52 per cent female. Notably, 87 per cent of male physicians with specialised qualifications were concentrated in Medicine and Surgery, whereas 96 per cent of female physicians with specialised qualifications held expertise in Obstetrics and Gynaecology. This research paper was published in the online medical journal PLOS ONE in January 2019. Speaking to Prothom Alo, Professor Syed Abdul Hamid of the Institute of Health Economics at Dhaka University noted that the academic excellence and advancement of female students represent a positive development. Academic records trapped in files: Our struggles in higher education According to him, they secure admission to medical colleges on the basis of merit through highly competitive entrance examinations. However, certain barriers persist in the professional workplace. Owing to working environments and logistical realities in rural and district-level areas, female physicians frequently encounter distinct challenges in performing their duties, he stated. Professor Abdul Hamid pointed out that female representation remains relatively low in several critical medical specialities as interest often remains concentrated in specific fields such as Obstetrics and Gynaecology. He stressed the importance of strategically encouraging broader female participation across diverse medical specialities to establish a balanced distribution, suggesting that the issue requires deliberation at the policy-making level.

title: Economy trapped in investment stagnation

article_text: A symptom often observed in many underdeveloped economies is when per capita income stalls at a stable equilibrium point. Although this income can meet the basic needs of living, it doesn't allow for savings or investments. Even if there is some surplus income, only a small portion flows into net investment channels. As capital resources such as factories, machinery, land, buildings, and natural resources grow, the population increases at an equal rate, so the amount of capital equipment or production inputs per worker does not increase. If the growth in per capita income is considered an indicator of economic growth, it can be said that these economies experience no growth. Such economies are said to be trapped in a ''low-level equilibrium trap.'' Seventy years ago, American economist Richard R Nelson presented the above theory to explain why underdeveloped or low-income countries often remain trapped in a long-standing cycle of poverty and stagnation. He suggested that a slight increase in per capita income might lead to a rise in birth rates or a decrease in death rates, causing the population growth rate to surpass the growth rate of total national income or capital formation, thus pulling down per capita income back to the previous minimum equilibrium level. This way, an economy gets trapped, and escaping becomes difficult. Recently, an analysis from the Power and Participation Research Centre (PPRC), a private research organisation, has suggested that Bangladesh's economy has fallen into a similar structural trap. Although this analysis does not refer specifically to Nelson's ''low-level equilibrium trap,'' it mentions three types of traps. The first is the tendency to rely on debt or break savings to cope with the family's financial distress. The second is the stagnation in investment leading to reduced GDP growth, and the third is the trap of political-administrative governance. The structural trap: How banking arbitrage starves our capital market The interconnected nature of these three traps has plunged the economy into a deep crisis. According to the organisation, a significant portion of the country's population, about 31 million people, is facing severe economic challenges. This class is in a ''fragile middle-class'' position, which can easily fall back into the poverty cycle. The rates of moderate and extreme poverty in the country have increased to 27. 9 per cent and 9. 35 per cent, respectively. Half of the families are struggling to meet regular medical expenses due to chronic illness, depleting their savings, and getting trapped in debt. Coupled with these symptoms is investment stagnation. As investments in both the public and private sectors have dropped, international organisations have significantly lowered their forecast for Bangladesh’s GDP growth. According to their estimates, the growth rate might fall to between 3 and 3.4 per cent. Government data also show the overall investment-to-GDP ratio in Bangladesh decreasing to 27.93 per cent in the 2025-26 fiscal year from 28.54 per cent the previous year. Due to this dismal investment rate, GDP growth has also declined. The government targets a 6.5 per cent GDP growth rate in the 2026-27 fiscal year, but the IMF forecasts it to be only 3.2 per cent, marking the lowest growth rate in the last 38 years. PPRC’s survey found that along with rising poverty rates, the general population is suffering from employment uncertainty, high inflation, and debt pressure. For several consecutive years, inflation has hovered around 10 per cent. Consequently, people's real income has been severely affected. The IMF believes that annual average inflation in Bangladesh will reach around 11 per cent in the current fiscal year, which would be the highest in the last 16 years. The annual average inflation in the 2010-11 fiscal year was 10.92 per cent. Another concern of PPRC is the governance trap. Sustainable development is consistently hindered due to structural weaknesses in political and governance systems. Weak revenue collection, heavy reliance on debt, political influence, and extreme inefficiency in government spending have led to the wastage of state resources. Our tax-to-GDP ratio is struggling to rise from between 6 and 7 per cent, leaving the government without enough revenue to spend on development, education, health, and social security. Thus, the government has to seek help from various donor organisations to meet budget expenses. Repayment of these loans later creates a shortage that requires taking more loans. In other words, we are constantly getting entangled in the debt trap instead of increasing revenue collection capacity. Why are people struggling in a country with a per capita income of 3000 dollars? Although Bangladesh is among the countries with a low tax-to-GDP ratio, there are other countries globally with an even lower ratio, such as Libya, Iraq, the United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain, oil-rich nations in the Arab and Middle Eastern regions. Because these countries' primary revenue comes from oil sales rather than the taxes of their citizens. Sudan, Yemen, and Ethiopia also have a lower tax-to-GDP ratio than ours. Sudan has gold and oil, and Yemen also has oil. However, due to economic mismanagement, administrative weaknesses, wars, etc. , these countries' tax-to-GDP ratios are also lower than Bangladesh’s. But this comparison should not suggest that the Arab countries' situation is worse than ours. PPRC's survey also expresses concern over Bangladesh's administrative inefficiencies regarding tax management. Whether referred to as Nelson's ''low-level equilibrium trap'' or PPRC's ''structural trap,'' Bangladesh’s current investment stagnation, rising poverty, declining GDP, and political-administrative weaknesses confirm the existence of both types of traps. PPRC has advised the government to acknowledge this reality because ignoring the disease never leads to its cure. To escape these traps, Nelson provided several suggestions. Given that the benefits of small investments are not realised under population growth pressure, ensuring the visible positive role of investments through extensive investments or a ''big push,'' attracting foreign direct investment, increasing productivity by applying modern and effective production methods, increasing employment compared to population growth to raise income growth rates, and encouraging savings and investment tendencies through social, political, and institutional reforms are essential. Among these reforms, it is possible to increase the efficiency and collection of revenue administration. Similarly, to break free from economic traps, PPRC suggests ensuring economic democracy and fair competition for all, establishing agriculture product processing, the pharmaceutical industry, light engineering, renewable energy supply systems, information technology, transportation-supply services, and care services as new growth drivers, enhancing technical skills and digital knowledge through quality education, providing opportunities for small businesses to grow into large and export-oriented establishments, and creating transparent, time-bound, digitally integrated rapid and accountable administration for public services. Notably, although some of these initiatives are long-term, in the short term, the most noteworthy strategy is to enhance people's incomes to increase purchasing power. Therefore, this should be given the highest priority. This should be combined with determined and effective efforts to increase investment instead of empty promises, providing opportunities to escape these traps. *Faruq Mainuddin is a writer and banker fmainuddin@hotmail. com *Opinions expressed here are the author's own. #This article, originally published in Prothom Alo print and online editions, has been rewritten in English by Rabiul Islam

title: You’ll amend the constitution, only for it to be whitewashed in court—we don’t agree: Jamaat Ameer
description: Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Ameer and Opposition Leader Shafiqur Rahman urged the government to abandon constitutional amendments and pursue reform, speaking at an event marking the July National Charter anniversary. He accused the BNP of forgetting past commitments, evading the Charter, and allegedly aligning with the banned Awami League. He criticised law and order, corruption, prices, and the Radda clinic attack, demanding justice. Other speakers called for implementing the July Charter and a constitutional reform council.
article_text: Opposition Leader and Ameer of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, Shafiqur Rahman, has urged the government to step back from amending the constitution. “Will you pass just another amendment? A court will completely whitewash it... We are not accustomed to, nor do we agree to, engaging in such futile efforts and persisting with the mistaken approaches of the past. That is precisely why we demand reform,” he stated. Shafiqur Rahman made these remarks while delivering his presidential address at a discussion organised by Jamaat-e-Islami at the Kazi Nazrul Islam Auditorium of the National Press Club in the capital on Sunday afternoon, marking the anniversary of the signing of the July National Charter. Addressing the ruling party, the Jamaat ameer said, “Why are you searching for the constitution now? To search for the constitution, you spent 15 and a half years holding a few meetings and rallies with the gracious permission of the government. Yet, you could not oust fascism. Neither could we, nor could you. That is the reality.” The Opposition Leader alleged that upon coming to power, BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) forgot the past. Shafiqur Rahman remarked that the government must break free from its mindset of amending the constitution. He stated that this constitution not only birthed fascism but also sought to give fascism a permanent structure. Shafiqur Rahman criticised the BNP’s stance on implementing the July National Charter. He noted that the BNP had expressed objections to significant reform proposals by issuing “notes of dissent”. Now, even the matters to which they had no objections are being evaded. The Jamaat ameer claimed that the BNP did not take a stance in favour of a “Yes” vote in the referendum. Instead, the party’s cadres both at home and abroad were instructed to vote “No”. However, that attempt failed due to the public verdict. Shafiqur Rahman expressed criticism over inviting the Opposition to discussions within the committee formed to amend the constitution. He remarked that they (the ruling party) had betrayed 70 per cent of the populace. The Opposition would not do that. The government will be compelled to implement this referendum. The Jamaat ameer also accused BNP of entering into an electoral understanding with Awami League (whose activities are banned in the country). He stated that during the election, BNP subtly begged for votes from Awami League. Sheikh Hasina and a godfather of the Awami League both mentioned this. A BNP Member of Parliament (MP) from Natore even thanked Awami League members for their success in the election. He further alleged that leaders from various organisations, including the Awami League, Jubo League, and Chhatra League, were given prominent positions within the BNP. Shafiqur Rahman raised questions regarding the law and order situation in the country. He asserted that if the government cannot prevent the influx of money, weapons, and drugs across the borders, it lacks the qualification to govern the country. The Opposition Leader noted that while the government announces various types of cards on one hand, people's lives have become miserable due to the burden of taxes and corruption on the other. The government lacks effective plans to rehabilitate returnee expatriates and restore comfort to the lives of ordinary citizens. The Jamaat ameer remarked that the prices of daily essentials are soaring due to extortion and illegal occupation. He cited that in Panchagarh, farmers sell four gourds for one taka, whereas consumers in Dhaka are forced to purchase a single gourd for 40 to 60 taka. Referring to the incident of attack, vandalism, and looting at the Radda MCH-FP Centre, a private maternal and child health clinic in Mirpur, Dhaka, Shafiqur Rahman stressed that the resignation of the concerned MP is not enough; she must be brought to justice under the law. Shafiqur Rahman also accused the government of subtly attempting to shift the blame onto the Opposition in an effort to cover up its monumental failures. Criticising the government’s anxiety regarding the Opposition’s programmes, Shafiqur Rahman asked why the government is so perturbed by the long march if it truly believes the programme lacks public support. He called on the government not to obstruct the Opposition’s activities or attempt to impose chaos upon them. The Jamaat ameer remarked that he has no objection if the prime minister consumes a lunch worth 100 to 150 taka. However, the government must ensure arrangements so that ordinary citizens can comfortably afford two square meals a day and live in peace. Speaking at the discussion, President of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), Colonel (retd) Oli Ahmad, said that Tarique Rahman must take lessons from the past. However, he warned that it is the people around the prime minister who will cause his downfall, and the prime minister cannot emerge victorious while fighting battles on all fronts. He urged the immediate announcement of the implementation of the July Charter in the public interest. Akhter Hossen, Member Secretary of the National Citizen Party (NCP), alleged that despite the legal foundation of the July Charter and the verdict of the referendum, the government wishes to reject the reform proposals. He stated that they (the BNP) now refuse to comply even with the proposals they previously agreed to, adding that the BNP has no desire to implement any reform agenda and is instead seeking pretexts to retreat. THe senior NCP leader asserted that the crisis must be resolved by dissolving the one-sided, single-party constitutional amendment committee and establishing a constitutional reform council in line with the referendum mandate. Mia Golam Porwar, Secretary General of Jamaat, remarked that the ground beneath the government’s feet has slipped away. Consequently, they are uttering nonsense and attempting to cling to power by misleading the nation. He added that an ill-fated attempt is being made to amend the constitution under the guise of a special committee, creating new narratives that run contrary to the spirit of the July Charter. Among others who addressed the discussion were Jamaat Nayeb-e-Ameer Mujeebur Rahman, Assistant Secretary General Hamidur Rahman Azad, Central Executive Council members Saiful Alam Khan (Milon), Nurul Islam Bulbul, and Salim Uddin; Jamaat Working Council member Shishir Monir; former diplomat Sakib Ali; AB Party Secretary Asaduzzaman Fuaad; President of Nexus Defence and Justice, Brigadier General (retd) Md. Hasan Nasir; retired army officer Hasinur Rahman; former DUJ President Elahi Newaz Khan; DUJ President Shahidul Islam; lawyer ASM Shahriar Kabir; and reserved seat MP and mother of July martyr Jabir Ibrahim, Rokeya Begum.

title: Syed Abul Maksud: Raconteur of Bangalee’s behaviour at micro level
description: Syed Abul Maksud wrote many books and articles based on his research and profuse study. Those range from philosophical musings to education, literature, social issues and feminism. He was a regular columnist to several newspapers and those articles were not just fillers, as I mentioned in the previous paragraph. In several cases, he was the first person to write books on the subjects he dealt with. His book on Sir Philip Joseph Hartog is one of such books. He also wrote a large book on Maulana Bhashani, who was one of the first persons from the then East Pakistan to say goodbye to West Pakistani rulers before the Liberation War in 1971. The Daily Star Books has published a collection of newspaper articles by Syed Abul Maksud under the title “Bangali Musalmaner Buddhibrittik Bibhrom O Biswashinota” in 2019. Some of the articles of the book are about the crème de la crème of the Bengali intellectuals and their sometimes deliberate and intentional contradictory behaviour. Such a revealing book is rare in Bangladesh.
article_text: A few days ago several of my colleagues and I were returning home by a CNG-run auto-rickshaw after our scheduled office time at night. It was around 11:30 pm. Any regular commuter on Dhaka roads knows this is not a peak hour for traffic, but not lean time either. This is such a time when drivers of public transports in Dhaka try to showcase their skill in speed after driving the vehicle rather slowly the whole day. At such a time, our auto-rickshaw driver was also not immune to the temptation. He showed his talent as sped past the Aarong Intersection at the western end of wide Manik Mia Avenue disobeying the traffic light. Awed, I just asked, “Bhai, what have you done! There was a red light there. You should have waited for the light to turn green.” The driver, however, in a rather casual tone answered, “Bhai, there is no traffic rule after 11:00 pm.” Listening to his response to my worries, I thought about reporting this to the supervisor of our office’s transport department. Maybe this could be a solution for one driver but what could be the remedy of this startling collective idea of transport drivers that “There is no traffic rule after 11:00 pm.” Upon reaching home, I disembarked the CNG-run auto-rickshaw and said to the driver, “Listen, you said ‘there is no traffic rule after 11:00 pm.’ What if another driver of a larger vehicle were there at that time and thought the same and violated the traffic lights. Could you imagine the result?” He did not feel the necessity to respond verbally to what I said. He just shrugged, closed the door of the backseat and went away. Standing there at the entrance of the building where I live, after a very long time I recalled some words I read in a newspaper article written by Syed Abul Maksud in Prothom Alo, most probably in 2007. He wrote, as far as I can remember, “It is very easy to call politicians names as they are easily identifiable because they are not even 1 per cent of the population. But the mass of people of more than 99 per cent remain hidden in a mist; we cannot identify them or hold them accountable for anything. It is this hidden mass that mostly defines the zeitgeist, not the otherwise.” Definitely I'm not absolving politicians of their accountabilities. Maybe, just maybe, you can correct the behaviour of one driver or a few drivers through punitive actions but what about the mass of not only transport drivers but normal youths and many others, who take pride in violating the traffic rules. The article presented a comparative discussion of actions by Bangalees during and after the Liberation War and the people of Vietnam after their war with the US. That article, more specifically the last few sentences of the article expanded my horizon to a great degree that would have otherwise taken a huge amount of reading and meditating on those for a rather long time. Once again, I realised the value of the life and writings of Syed Abul Maksud, who was rather laconic, as has been described by his friends and acquaintances. Syed Abul Maksud wrote many books and articles based on his research and profuse study. Those range from philosophical musings to education, literature, social issues and feminism. He was also a regular columnist to several newspapers and those articles were not just fillers. In several cases, he was the first person to write books on the subjects he dealt with. His book on Sir Philip Joseph Hartog is one of such books. He also wrote a large book on Maulana Bhashani, who was one of the first persons from the then East Pakistan to say goodbye to West Pakistani rulers before the Liberation War in 1971. The Daily Star Books has published a collection of newspaper articles by Syed Abul Maksud under the title “Bangali Musalmaner Buddhibrittik Bibhrom O Biswashinota” in 2019. Some of the articles of the book are about the crème de la crème of the Bengali intellectuals and their sometimes deliberate and intentional contradictory behaviour. Such a revealing book is rare in Bangladesh. But he was not just a man of letters; he was an upright and a man of words too. He was a news editor at the state-run news agency, Bangladesh Sangbad Sangsatha (BSS) in 2004. At that time he wrote a scathing article in a newspaper on the attack on writer and Dhaka University professor Humayun Azad. The article invoked the ire of the then information minister and the prime minister’s political affairs adviser. They advised Syed Abul Maksud not to publish such columns. In protest, he resigned from the news agency job in just 15 minutes of receiving the “advice”. Later, he wrote, “If I were to choose between writing and a job, I would love to always choose the first one.” 23 October 2026 was the 80th birthday of Syed Abul Maksud, who breathed his last in 2021. A few newspaper articles were published by a handful of newspapers commemorating his birthday. But it passed mostly silently. It was not so unexpected though. But it would be better for us if we remember him and study his writings. They surely will help us in times like today.

title: The mistake keeping Bangladesh from tapping into Japan’s labour market
description: Japan’s labour shortage, driven by its ageing population, has created a major opportunity for Bangladesh. However, we have fallen behind due to gaps in skills, Japanese-language proficiency and demand-driven training. By measuring labour migration in terms of numbers rather than skills, failing to formulate effective policies and plan ahead, and being unable to build effective partnerships with employers, we have failed to turn our demographic advantage into sustainable employment despite having a large young population. There are several clear examples of Bangladesh’s past failures in accessing Japan’s labour market. In July 2005, an agreement between Bangladesh and Japan was signed to create opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to receive technical training and work in Japan. However, over the following eight years, Bangladesh managed to send only 41 workers to Japan under the agreement—12 through the government agency, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), and 29 through private recruitment agencies. This was an embarrassing example of policy failure on Bangladesh’s part. Yet Japanese small and medium-sized enterprises had a demand for Bangladeshi workers. Inadequate language skills, inappropriate worker selection, lengthy administrative procedures and a lack of coordination among the organisations concerned stood in the way of capitalising on that opportunity. Our failure to move forward was not due to a lack of opportunities, but rather an inability to turn those opportunities into actual employment.
article_text: Japan’s labour shortage, driven by its ageing population, has created a major opportunity for Bangladesh. However, we have fallen behind due to gaps in skills, Japanese-language proficiency and demand-driven training. By measuring labour migration in terms of numbers rather than skills, failing to formulate effective policies and plan ahead, and being unable to build effective partnerships with employers, we have failed to turn our demographic advantage into sustainable employment despite having a large young population. There are several clear examples of Bangladesh’s past failures in accessing Japan’s labour market. In July 2005, an agreement between Bangladesh and Japan was signed to create opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to receive technical training and work in Japan. However, over the following eight years, Bangladesh managed to send only 41 workers to Japan under the agreement, 12 through the government agency, the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET), and 29 through private recruitment agencies. This was an embarrassing example of policy failure on Bangladesh’s part. Yet Japanese small and medium-sized enterprises had a demand for Bangladeshi workers. Inadequate language skills, inappropriate worker selection, lengthy administrative procedures and a lack of coordination among the organisations concerned stood in the way of capitalising on that opportunity. Our failure to move forward was not due to a lack of opportunities, but rather an inability to turn those opportunities into actual employment. Although an agreement was reached with Japan’s IM Japan in 2015 to train 500 Bangladeshis, and a new initiative was launched in 2017 to provide one-year training in the manufacturing and construction sectors, Bangladesh failed to demonstrate the capacity to turn these initiatives into large-scale, sustained employment programmes. Even after Bangladesh signed a memorandum of cooperation with Japan on a framework for sending Specified Skilled Workers (SSW) on August 27, 2019, overcoming limitations in language education, skills assessment and transparent recruitment has remained an urgent priority. More significantly, surveys conducted by Japan’s immigration authorities among technical trainees from various countries have revealed that many fall into debt after paying large sums of money to recruitment agencies and intermediaries in their home countries. In light of this risk, Bangladesh’s failure to establish a transparent and accountable recruitment system needs to be reassessed. These experiences demonstrate that signing a memorandum of understanding is not, in itself, a measure of success. True success lies in translating such agreements into skilled workers, lower migration costs and sustainable employment. What Bangladesh can gain from PM's Japan visit First mistake: Training before demand, investment without job guarantees One of the major weaknesses of Bangladesh’s labour export system is the disconnect between training and actual recruitment. Training programmes should be designed based on data showing how many workers are needed in each sector, what qualifications employers require and which skills tests candidates must pass. However, the tendency to measure success by the number of training centres, trainees or certificates issued has obscured the actual outcomes. Learning Japanese, acquiring professional skills and passing qualification tests are time-consuming processes. When training centres vary in quality and there are no genuine employment opportunities after training, young people end up wasting both time and money. As a result, many aspiring to work in Japan fall behind even at the preparation stage. The question is: why has Bangladesh not done enough to establish partnerships with Japanese employers and introduce training programmes tailored to their needs? Why has the country failed to develop the capacity to assess demand in foreign labour markets based on data rather than assumptions? This failure cannot be attributed to any one individual; it reflects longstanding weaknesses in policymaking and institutional management. Second Mistake: Failing to treat language as a core skill requirement Japanese-language proficiency is not merely an additional qualification for working in Japan. It is essential for understanding workplace instructions, communicating with colleagues, maintaining safety and managing daily life. Yet Bangladesh has failed to make the expected progress in establishing a comprehensive system that makes Japanese-language education accessible, affordable and of consistent quality. The concentration of opportunities in Dhaka, high training costs and a shortage of qualified teachers create barriers for prospective workers. For a young person in a rural area, covering the costs of language classes, examinations and documentation can often be difficult. In other words, in a labour market where preparation is crucial for entry, access to that preparation is not equal for everyone. The state’s responsibility was not simply to establish training centres, but to integrate language education, vocational training and recruitment into a single system. The absence of such a coordinated approach has put Bangladesh at a disadvantage. Third mistake: Failing to establish a reliable, low-cost recruitment system Complaints about intermediaries, opaque fees, fraud and excessive costs have long plagued Bangladesh’s migration system. Preparing to enter a market such as Japan is already expensive. When uncertainty over recruitment is added to the equation, the risks for young workers and their families increase manifold. Japanese employers, meanwhile, want partners who can reliably provide suitable workers. If Bangladesh cannot ensure transparent recruitment, verified training and reasonable costs, it cannot gain a competitive advantage simply by virtue of its abundant workforce. Our mistake has been to leave migration largely dependent on individuals’ own initiative and financial capacity. The state, however, should have taken responsibility for controlling recruitment costs, effectively monitoring licensed recruitment agencies and establishing channels for direct engagement with foreign employers. When workers fall into debt before even leaving for a job abroad, much of the benefit of securing higher-paying employment is undermined. Fourth mistake: Failing to recognise the importance of competitors Bangladesh is not alone in Japan’s labour market. Other labour-sending countries are also working to expand language education, technical training and cooperation with employers. Some benefit from decades of labour migration experience, established recruitment networks and familiarity with the Japanese language and culture. Bangladesh’s policymakers should have analysed the experiences of competing countries to identify the country’s own weaknesses. A sustained strategy was needed to determine which sectors offer Bangladesh a comparative advantage, where training needs to be expanded and how employers’ confidence could be earned. However, the complacency associated with being a major labour-sending country prevented us from fully appreciating the importance of such competitive preparation. What is needed now is accountability, not promises To overcome these failures, the first step should be to develop a five-year action plan for Japan’s labour market, with measurable targets. Clear indicators must specify how many workers are to be sent to Japan in each sector, how many will receive language and skills training, how many will secure jobs and how many will remain employed. The performance of training institutions must be measured not by the number of certificates issued, but by actual employment outcomes and workers’ earnings. Direct partnerships must be established with Japanese employers, industry associations and training institutions. At the same time, access to language education and skills testing must be expanded beyond Dhaka, financial assistance for training must be provided, recruitment costs must be fully disclosed, and swift action must be taken against fraud. Employment contracts must clearly specify wages, working hours, accommodation costs and procedures for filing complaints. Bangladeshis working abroad must also have access to legal assistance in Bangla and an effective grievance redress mechanism. Most importantly, diplomatic visits and memorandums of understanding must not be presented as substitutes for success. Success should be measured by how many Bangladeshis actually secure decent jobs, how little they have to spend to migrate and how safely they can work abroad. Japan’s labour market presents a major opportunity for Bangladesh, but there is no guarantee that this window of opportunity will remain open indefinitely. Unless we learn from past mistakes, new initiatives will simply repeat old failures. Bangladesh must establish itself not as a source of cheap labour, but as a partner capable of delivering skilled, reliable workers while safeguarding their rights. The question, therefore, is not merely how many workers Bangladesh can send to Japan. It is whether, having failed for so long to adequately prepare despite the opportunities available, we now have the political will to take responsibility for those failures and correct them. * Dr Selim Reza is an associate professor and coordinator of the Centre for Migration Studies (CMS) at North South University. * The views expressed here are the author’s own. * This article has been translated into English by Ayesha Kabir

title: ‘Honey trap’ gang lures wealthy men into rooms, then blackmails them
description: The scheme began with introductions on social media, where the suspects gradually built fake romantic relationships with their targets before luring them to designated apartments or hotel rooms.
